speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Martineau (Parliameniary Secretary to the Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MR. MARTINEAU    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 10
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a matter of privilege, yesterday the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) made a speech in this house. He referred in particular to the constituency of Pontiac-Temis-camingue, which I represent, and to one polling division in that constituency where he stated that a large number of Indian voters who were on the 1958 voters' list had not exercised their right of franchise. He stated that the reason they had not done so was that on election day they were in no condition to vote due to the fact-to use the hon. member's own words-that they had been plied with liquor. This is reported at page 1934 of yesterday's Hansard.
Mr. Speaker, this is clearly a reflection on certain constituents in my riding and is also clearly a reflection on my honour as a member of this house. I wish to state in unequivocal terms that the words used by the hon. member for Gatineau do not represent the facts as they are known to me. I therefore deny that I or any of my agents or anybody for whom I may have had any responsibility ever did prevent, through liquor or by any other means, anybody in my constituency from exercising their franchise.
It is true that there were a large number of voters on the list who did not vote. The reason was that when the enumeration was taken there were a number of bush workers who did not live at Forbes Depot but who happened to be there and whose names were included on the voters' list. When election time came many of them had left that neighbourhood because the bush operations were terminated, and they probably voted elsewhere in my constituency or in neighbouring constituencies.
I wish to repeat with emphasis that never did I prevent anyone from voting. Everyone was encouraged to vote. That was our set policy, and if there were voters who did not vote it did not spring from any act on my part. Moreover, I resent the implication made on my constituents.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. MARTINEAU    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 10
speechtext:
I take it the hon. member is satisfied with having made his explanation, and that he was not in the house at the time the statement was made or he would have made his explanation at that time. I was in the chair and heard the statement, but I did not take from what was said any identification of the parliamentary secretary with what was said by the hon. member for Gatineau. However, if he understood that there was an insinuation against himself, he has now made his explanation and perhaps the hon. member whose statement is complained of wishes to say something before the matter is closed.
(Translation):

subtopic: MR. MARTINEAU    REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 10
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have heard what the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) has just said. I have not sought to accuse either the elected member or the defeated candidate. I simply noted the fact that, as I said, the Indians were served intoxicating beverages and that many of them were unable to vote because they were in no condition to get to the polls. That is what I said.
I said nothing against the member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue. There were two candidates in that election. I did not say it was the member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue, nor did I say that it was the defeated candidate, who supplied the liquor. The fact remains however, that a few days before the elections, the Indians started drinking liquor that was surely supplied by someone.

speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether he will take steps to ensure that the defence estimates are introduced in the house at the earliest possible date, so we may have a discussion of defence policy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I am most desirous of seeing these matters advanced, but as a matter of fact there are a number of legislative items on the order paper which have to receive the attention of parliament at the earliest possible date.
At the moment what we are trying to do is clear up these matters of legislation, to the end that the discussion which the hon. gentleman has in mind, and other matters, may be dealt with. At this time I do not intend to say more than this; that over the years I have been strongly opposed to holding two sittings a year, and I hope we shall be able to advance this legislative program. Otherwise-and there is no criticism in this whatsoever-at the rate progress is being made I would think my views expressed in the past against two sittings a year may have to be changed. I point that out simply for the record, because after all we are now in our forty-second day and the order paper does not seem to be diminishing at any great rate of speed. I hope that after a number of matters are dealt with in the legislative program the subject of defence may receive early attention in committee.

The house resumed, from Thursday, March 10, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Walker-Mr. Flynn in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1954 to increase the aggregate amount of all loans in respect of which insurance policies may he issued under the act from four billion dollars to six billion dollars; and to increase from one billion dollars to one and a half billion dollars the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund for the purposes specified in subsection 1 of section 22 of the said act.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before proceeding with my remarks I must take this first opportunity to congratulate the minister on his appointment, and wish him all success in everything he undertakes to the general advantage of the people of this country. I certainly hope he proves to be the ministerial David who will slay the Goliath of short credit for housing.
We socialists believe the virtue of any nation is nourished by good homes. Satisfactory housing is essential for our people. Sometimes when I listen to hon. members of the opposition and have private discussions with them I realize that they have misconceptions as to the purposes and objectives of the socialist philosophy, and what the purpose of a socialist is with respect to giving expression to that philosophy. As a matter of fact some of them get an appalling idea of what socialist objectives are. They appear to think we are aiming to bring about a state of affairs where multitudes of warm bodies and full bellies will be living in a bliss of togetherness singing "I'm forever blowing bubbles", or something of that sort. We as socialists believe in the sanctity and the dignity of the individual. This is one reason we are concerned about housing and good homes. In our opinion, socialism is not all a question of bread and butter. It

is not a question of material things. Material things are only a step toward a better life for all our people.
In my opinion socialism is a search for truth, a worship of beauty-and beauty in all its forms-for the purpose of creating an environment where goodness will generally prevail. As socialists we believe that good homes are the foundation for that ideal. I am one of those people who believe that a man's home is his castle and a place where character, virtue, ideals and loyalty are fostered to the advantage of the public welfare. It is for this reason that our people are particularly interested in housing.
Now, Mr. Chairman, other members of our group have dealt at some length with the financial aspects of this problem. I am not going to take the time of the committee to repeat what they have had to say, except to emphasize that in my opinion there are two things that should be given particular consideration when it comes to credit. In my opinion, in agriculture and housing, if their needs are to be met in both instances, there should be opportunity for long term low interest loans. That type of credit is so important that even if it requires a measure of subsidization from the federal and the provincial governments-and in some cases it is justified on the municipal basis-it should be forthcoming.
I am pleased to note that the inquiry recently carried on by the royal architectural institute of Canada was made possible by a grant of $30,000 from the government. That was a very good investment indeed. It gives the officers and members of this organization an opportunity to make a study of this problem across the country, which they have been doing, and to get the opinions of wide sections of the people, both professional, those interested in the building of houses, and also those interested in obtaining houses, town planning, and so on. I am sure all of us will look forward to the report that will result from the investigation.
I want to say a word or two on the question of community planning, because we see such shocking need for it across the whole country. We can understand the lack of planning prior to the second world war particularly. Ideas had not developed along those lines to any great extent in a large portion of this country, but it is almost incomprehensible to me to see the lack of community planning that has existed since the second world war and the mistakes that have been made particularly in some of the larger centres, in connection with housing developments. In my opinion it is not only a question of this government's action, but there
National Housing Act
has to be co-operation among the federal, provincial and municipal governments to give effect to satisfactory programs for community planning. A lot of education has to be done in that line; there has to be an appreciation of the need for community planning on the part of a larger number of people; there has to be a larger number of people who are offended by the ugliness or the lack of planning that exists in this country today.
There are quite a number of agencies other than government which can play an effective role in this respect. In this connection I do urge that the minister, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and others use their opportunities to as great an extent as possible to give guidance, information and direction along those lines. Naturally I realize they are limited to some extent in so far as provincial and municipal authorities are concerned, but I think they can do a great deal more to promote the understanding of the necessity for community planning in Canada at this time.
We have seen a terrific increase in the cost of housing, with a great increase in the cost of land resulting from the greed of speculators, and in some cases not from greed but just from the natural increase in values because of the pressures of population and that sort of thing. I understand that in some instances Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have purchased land in various places in anticipation of development; in some instances to advantage and, I understand, in some instances the choice has not proven wise. I understand private builders are possibly going to purchase some of these properties for their own building projects. However, this is something we must keep in mind. A great deal more planning and assessment of future needs must be undertaken if we are to have community planning and the space for development in the future without ugliness, without dreariness, without shabbiness and all the things that go with them.
I must say a word or two about low rental housing, because this is one of the primary needs in housing in Canada, particularly for older people. "While a great deal has been done to date, there is a great deal more required if we are to build the low rental housing required by workers because of the mobility of their employment, and things of that sort, and also provide for the needs of our older people.
I am very pleased at this time to say that there has been co-operation by the federal and provincial governments with the municipality of Trail in connection with urban redevelopment. There is a good illustration

National Housing Act
of the ugliness that has developed over the years in a community that has produced millions in profits. No one person is responsible; it just grew like Topsy. I am glad to know that the survey was made possible as the result of the grant of the federal government, that both the provincial government and municipal authorities are co-operating and that a satisfactory report has been made as a result of the survey.
When you come to redevelop areas within cities, as in this case, that are the result of years of haphazard growth and development, it is a very expensive thing. While there is a will on all sides to change the situation, it is going to be very expensive indeed. I hope the answer to redevelopment in Trail will come soon. These problems surely should be lessons for us at this time not to repeat the mistakes of the past.
I want to say a word about small communities, because I am a country man and have lived in the country all my life. I was born in London, but that was only because my mother was there on that day. I have always enjoyed country life, and I think we fail to appreciate the contribution toward the settlement of many of these problems that the small communities can make. I am looking forward to the decentralization of industry instead of it being hived up in a small space as it is in that ever-expanding city of Toronto, and in other cities in Canada. Let us make greater use of the small communities. With improved transportation facilities, particularly improved highways, I am sure a great deal more can be done to dencentralize secondary industry.
As I said before, I think opportunities have been overlooked in the small communities for the provision of homes for the retired, the elderly. I have done a bit of promotion in that regard myself. I go about beating the drum for the small communities in my own constituency There are beautiful communities in ideal locations that I am sure most members of the house would envy. Yet if there is not something done, if there is not some guidance, if there is not some prodding, then in many cases people will retire from industry and continue to live their lives under somewhat squalid circumstances that are not always occasioned by lack of funds and things of that sort.
I have been able to get a good number of people to move to smaller places, villages of 500, 1,000, 250 or in some cases with a population of 150. Pensioners can build their own homes much more cheaply under these circumstances, and enjoy the type of life provided there. Today most of these communities have electric light and power, facilities that did not exist years ago. I suggest
[Mr. Herridge.l
to the minister that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could do more in that respect. Private lenders are a bit shy when it comes to these small communities, and while I do not criticize the officials of the corporation generally, because I think they have done a great job through the years under very difficult circumstances, I think there has been a tendency on the part of the corporation not to fully recognize this need, and plan for the future.
I urge that special consideration be given to assessing the opportunities in small communities all across Canada, in order to see what can be done to enable retired and elderly people particularly to build houses in these communities so they may live to better advantage and to the advantage and development of the communities concerned. It is going to take a bit of guidance on the part of the government, the corporation and the provincial and municipal authorities, and certainly some promotion.
I have gone to a man and said, "Look here, where do you intend to retire", and he has said, "I am going to stay here". I have said, "Come up to our part of the country and I will take you around and show you some cheap lots that you can get from the government for $50." They did not know those lots were there. You can get lumber for $30 a thousand, because third grade lumber is just as good as first grade for certain uses. People can build small homes there and live satisfactory lives. They can cut their own wood for fuel and spend their summer days fishing and gardening. But all this takes guidance and information. There are abundant opportunities in the smaller places if only they were brought to the attention of those who would be very pleased to retire and live under such circumstances.
There is one other matter I should like to mention. I have been very impressed with the good work that is being done under the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act. I think it has been our outstanding housing program in Canada. To start with it was not intended as a housing program but as a sort of subsistence farming arrangement. That is not how it works out, but that does not make any difference. It does provide an opportunity for men to build their own homes, to cultivate their half acre of ground, to get the pleasure that comes from association with mother earth, nature and so on, and to reduce their cost of living in that way.
I think the minister should give consideration to the development of a program something like the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act, with particular application to the smaller communities throughout

the country. When you have the type of person, the type of character and personality who delights in going into a small community and enjoys that sort of thing, then I say that nine times out of ten you have a very stable person. You are not dealing with someone who is going to assume an obligation today and forget about it tomorrow. I suggest that consideration should be given to a program somewhat along the line of the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act whereby suitable people would have the opportunity to build their own homes by being their own contractors.
There has been a tremendous change in housing in the last 50 or 75 years. What a difference. It makes me conscious of the problem that faces many young families today as compared with 50, 75 or 100 years ago. I grew up as a boy in a district where you could build your house out of the natural products around you. I know a person in my constituency who within the last 25 years has built a beautiful log home out of the forest, a log home with 4,000 feet of floor space. Everything that went into the home, stone, gravel, logs, lumber, beautiful flooring of different species in the different rooms, came off the property, and all this at a cost of less than $7,000. It is a poem in wood and local stone for less than $7,000, and with 4,000 feet of floor space. That shows you what can be done if you live under such circumstances.
But the majority of our people do not live under these circumstances, and for that reason I realize that we have a particular responsibility to those who, not living under these circumstances, must build their houses under much more expensive and artificial conditions. Yet I must say in passing that I think we overlook the opportunities in that respect in some parts of Canada. I am just speaking from experience. I happen to know a young man who was very interested in settling in the country. He was going to send away for lumber, asphalt shingles and so on. I took him and showed him what could be done with logs and local materials. He has built a beautiful home with a shake roof at a fraction of the cost, and it is a much more artistic and solidly built home than he could have built from imported products. I think something can be done in that direction. I do not say this can be done on a large scale, but there are opportunities for that type of construction and I suggest that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should have a few plans showing how to build a satisfactory log home.
I want to say a word or two about materials, because I find there is a great deal of ignorance in that regard. People generally are buying wallboard, gyproc, lumber and 79951-0-125
National Housing Act
other things without much knowledge of what they are purchasing. I suggest that something further could be done to create an interest in Canadian products. I do not want to appear to be touting the lumber business because I happen to be associated with a microscopic lumber company, but I think something should be done with respect to informing people as to the uses of lumber and what can be done with low grade lumber. We have No. 1 common, No. 2 common, No. 3, culls and so on. When it comes to building a home there is no need for a man to buy No. 1 common lumber for the walls when he is going to put gyproc on top. Generally speaking you can buy No. 3 lumber and in some cases culls at a fraction of the cost and have an equally satisfactory structure. All that is required is to cut out some of the knotholes and possibly cut off six inches of waste here and there, and so on. A great deal can be done to inform people of the uses of lumber and what can be done with certain grades. Then there is the question of variety in housing. I am a bit of an individualist. I suppose I could be called a socialist individualist.

I believe in individual design, but we seem to be living in an age of mass production. I think we should give some consideration to the esthetic value when it comes to housing, because there is no question but that a good home surrounded by lawns and gardens has an effect on character so far as children are concerned. The younger generation get their ideas as far as beauty is concerned, whether in music, art, housing or public buildings, from the things they hear and see. I feel we have a responsibility to indicate that we have some interest in developing the beautiful as well as building the useful.
I do suggest that there could be a greater variety of plans. You can go into so many houses and find that while they are warm and comfortable, they are very much alike. It may happen that the dining room is on the left side of the front door instead of the right; the roof may be green instead of blue, but fundamentally they are very much alike. You may find the same chrome furniture, which I dislike because I am very fond of the grain and colour of wooden things. I do believe something can be done to develop variety in housing. Variety results in a sense of pride because your house is different from the other chap's. This is a deep-seated instinct in human nature. As I said before, only the socialists realize that the bread and butter issues are only foundations on which we build.

National Housing Act
Now we come to the question of price. I think something could be done, given an understanding of the opportunities in the various materials, the variety of materials and the grades that are necessary, to reduce the price of housing to many people.
I have spoken, Mr. Chairman, in rather general terms because I did not want to repeat what has been said by previous speakers in this group. I do think if we give consideration to some of the things I have suggested we will improve the housing program in Canada. We can do something to lower the cost, even under present conditions. We can introduce a variety which will bring a greater degree of beauty into our housing developments, and by doing that not only will we be building houses but we will be providing homes that are the basis for a sound society.

speechtext: I have listened with great interest to the speech of the hon. member, and I want to ask him a question. He has spoken about guidance, and I was very interested in that point. I want to ask him just how he thinks this guidance can be provided, and by whom. Central mortgage is primarily a lending institution. I would be interested, and I am sure the minister would, if the hon. member could indicate from where he thinks this guidance should come; because I am sure we all think it is highly desirable and something we would like to see furnished if possible.

X am glad to attempt to answer the hon. member's question. We look upon Central Mortgage and Housing as more than a lending institution. It is the people of Canada's institution responsible for providing housing and, consequently, homes in Canada. I think it has recognized its responsibility as more than a lending institution by the character of the booklets it has published and the plans it has circulated.
When it comes to guidance, I always think you can work through local organizations. I am talking about the small community, possibly in some cases not incorporated. I am thinking of one in particular. I feel that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or other appropriate government agencies, either federal or provincial, could work in co-operation with local organizations. I find that women's institutes and women's organizations are particularly effective in that respect. They will meet together and get some literature for a series of studies. I know that women's institutes have undertaken a good deal in that direction in the smaller places where the women are not distracted by a multitude of engagements such as cocktail parties and that sort of activity. There is

a good deal that could be done without imposing any instructions from a higher authority. As I said before, we should give some guidance to people who are anxious to act but who are not well enough informed to be able to act until they get some guidance and information.

Mr. Chairman, I consider it my duty to say a few words in support of this motion, introduced in committee of the whole house by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), and to congratulate and thank our government, on behalf of my electors, for its interest in housing and unemployment problems, and for the assistance it is offering to solve those problems.
I have the honour to represent Quebec West, a constituency peopled almost exclusively by workers in all sorts of trades and by labourers. Some of them work in small and medium industries, in particular the shoe industry, but most of them are construction workers, that is to say carpenters, plumbers, electricians, painters, etc.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, wintertime is a particularly difficult and hard period in my constituency, especially for construction workers and labourers. The index of building activity seems to be slightly down compared to last year. Individual money lenders are fewer and more demanding in the way of collateral, terms and interest rates.
It is well known that banks and credit unions have also had to restrict credit and loans in order to curb inflation. Like my hon. friend and colleague from the constituency of Levis (Mr. Bourget), I wish to pay special tribute to our credit unions, our caisses populates for the great services they have rendered in the past years in the field of construction, by granting loans at reasonable rates and at conditions that could be met by the borrowers.
It is therefore, with great satisfaction, Mr. Chairman, that I support this resolution raising from $1 billion to $1J billion the total amount which may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund, so that the C.M.H.C. can guarantee building loans for low rental or family units.
I have been a practitioner for more than 38 years among those good working people that I know so well for their honesty and thrift.
Forty or more years ago, in spite of low wages and seasonal unemployment, many of those workers, who, at the time, did not have to contend with taxes of all kinds which have burdened them for many years now, managed to lay money aside and build themselves small homes. But due to the demands of today's economy, they cannot always make

ends meet. In many cases they can meet their obligations only by selling their small house and lot.
What they must do, therefore, is to find low rental accommodation. Thus the building of those multi-unit homes renting at prices they can afford to pay, is a boon to them.
In my riding, Quebec West, a building project for 700 such housing units, the Duberge Patios, was partially completed last year for 168 families of small wage earners whose individual revenue was under $2,500 a year. Those housing units are carefully built under the close supervision of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and so planned as to promote health and outdoor activities, each family having a yard and access to community playgrounds and recreation facilities.
A mixed school is now under construction to provide for the needs of that budding parish. I therefore would ask the Minister of Public Works to be so kind as to authorize the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to grant out of the $500 million mentioned in this resolution, a further loan for another 150 housing units, so as to carry on the fine project launched by the Duberge Patios. The demand for low rental housing still being very strong, those units will be rented as soon as they are completed. The promoters of the project have already laid plans for a shopping centre. They are also considering building a church in order to complete the project by creating a new parish of comfortably housed workers who will be perfectly organized in every respect.
This building activity will, at the same time, create jobs for all those good workers in my riding who would rather earn their bread than beg for it, or eat it thinly sliced out of their unemployment insurance benefits.
In those few remarks, I referred only to low rental housing. I also would like to suggest that loans be granted for small single family units, for people whose incomes vary between $3,000 and $5,000 and which would constitute a class of small owners. For some time, new and cheaper materials are available and simplified building procedures have cut down the cost of putting up a dwelling.
With longer terms granted for payment and with the 3 per cent refund which the government of the province of Quebec will extend, as from this year, on C.M.H.C. loans, it would be possible, it seems to me, to extend to our people more generous and flexible loans.

I should like, at this time, to call the attention of hon. members of the house, and in particular of the Minister of Public Works, to what appears to me to be a deficiency in the legislation governing the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In fact, according to that legislation, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation protects only the general contractor who builds the house whose construction costs it guarantees, but it completely overlooks the subcontractors. If the general contractor is honest and solvent, there is no problem, but it is not always so. Subcontractors in plumbing, wiring, sash and doors, painting or landscaping have told me they have lost one, two or even three thousand dollars to some dishonest or financially unreliable general contractor.
Some of my colleagues in the house have told me of similar complaints they have received. Unable as they were to take out liens to protect themselves, those subcontractors have lost their claims. This legislation should therefore be amended, if necessary, so as to allow and even oblige Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to require from the general contractor, before he is paid in full, that he show receipts proving that the subcontractors have been paid in full or, at least, guaranteed payment of their share.
The housing shortage for large families has developed into a very serious problem. I am not against a sound immigration policy, but, before drawing people from Europe to fill Canada, I think we might appropriately start with settling our own people.
Families of seven, eight or more children are hard put to find suitable accommodation, yet such families supply us with some of our best citizens.
It is in large families that the virtues of sacrifice and generosity are best honoured and best observed. Those families are therefore the best source to draw from to populate the country. My suggestion, therefore, is that loan regulations be made more flexible, and even more generous, so as to help large families organize their home.
May I add, Mr. Chairman, that not only will this $500 million that is being made available for housing help relieve unemployment but will give real impetus to Canadian economy in general.
In all countries, construction is considered a vital industry, one that keeps alive the whole range of related industries and of all kinds of commercial enterprises.

National Housing Act
Especially does the housing industry provide individuals and families with prosperity and comfort and also with physical and mental health. Is this not a source of wealth for a country?
In civilized countries, or in countries that we seek to develop, we should eliminate improper shelter for animals, and, all the more so, improper housing for humans.
So, I congratulate the Minister of Public Works for the resolution he is introducing in order to help solve the thorny problem of housing, a resolution which is perfectly in accord with the progressive policies of our government in all fields.
I conclude with these words from a well known and very realistic French song: "When the building trade flourishes, everything flourishes."
Once again, I heartily support the resolution of the Minister of Public Works. I congratulate him and thank him for proposing it to us, thus giving me an opportunity to make my modest contribution.

While this resolution is under discussion I welcome the opportunity to mention some of the housing needs in my district, and I should like to call attention to the Goose Bay area in Labrador. Originally when the airport at Goose Bay was under construction many workers went there with a view to obtaining temporary employment, but as time went on they began to settle there. The result is that a large community has grown up within a few miles of the Goose Bay airport. This is the community of Happy Valley. The large numbers of personnel employed in various phases of the Goose Bay airport operation and the number of people who have settled in its proximity make it desirable to examine carefully the housing problem in this area.
I should like to call the attention of the minister to this problem and invite him to give it his sympathetic study and find out what has been done toward making provision for a housing development in the Goose Bay-Happy Valley area.
Further south in my constituency, in the mining area at Tilt Cove in Green Bay, Newfoundland, a road has been built between Tilt Cove and the town of La Scie just a few miles away. Room for housing is restricted at Tilt Cove, where the mine is located, and
[Mr. Bissonnette.l
a development at the town of La Scie would appear to be the answer. I should like to ask the minister what progress, if any, has been made toward a housing development at La Scie. A new mining development is also under way at Little Bay in Green Bay.

speechtext:
I wish to make a few remarks, particularly in respect to housing needs in the Toronto area.
First of all I wish to congratulate the minister on his appointment as Minister of Public Works. I know that from his own experience in Toronto he understands the housing needs of that city as well as I do, if not better. At the same time there are a few things I should like to put on record, because one sometimes feels that there are those who underestimate the continuing need for housing, especially when they see certain houses being built without buyers found for them.
I think we should congratulate the government on the assistance it has given to hous-

ing to date. I know that during the two years in which the present government has been in power it has done nine times more than the former administration did to encourage housing under the type of assistance provided by the resolution now under discussion.
In the city of Toronto an official plan of the metropolitan area has been prepared setting out what are considered to be housing needs until 1980. Officials have estimated that because of the rise in incomes, more families and more single persons, or groups of single persons, will be in a position to establish their own households. In 1958, on an average, 1,000 persons occupied 257 dwelling units. In 1980 it is estimated that the same number of people will require 278 dwelling units. In addition, new dwelling units will be required to replace those lost by demolition and deconversion, and it is estimated that to deal with the situation the housing stock will grow from 417,000 units in 1958 to 791,000 units in 1980, an increase of 89 per cent. About 40,000 dwelling units will be demolished, but 20,000 will be added by conversion. About 395,000 units, or half of all the dwelling units existing in 1980, will be new structures. Because of this development it is expected that in 1980 there will be 177,200 apartments containing six or more suites. Apartments will account for 22 per cent as compared with 14 per cent of all dwelling units in the planning area at the present time.
In spite of the expected rise in the level of real family income there will be large sections of the population unable to buy or rent the new units-elderly persons and those whose income standards are low, for example-and to meet this most urgent need the plan proposes that a public housing program involving at least 1,000 family units and 500 units for elderly persons should be carried out annually.
I have brought this to the attention of the committee in order to set out some of the anticipated needs in the Toronto area. In addition one has to take into consideration the need for maintaining or redeveloping the older sections in the city of Toronto, and this makes it imperative to continue a program of conservation and rehabilitation.
I would be remiss if I did not state that in the city of Toronto we feel that our civic authorities have been leaders in the field of housing redevelopment. In the minister's
National Housing Act
own riding the Regent Park development has been one of the first to be carried out since the end of the second world war, and has been a success. Other areas are being developed. The Lawrence Heights area development has been completed. In addition, housing for elderly persons has been given great encouragement. One of the largest units is West Lodge, now named after Alderman May Robinson. Mrs. Robinson, who has done a great deal for elderly persons in the city of Toronto, well merits that these units should be named after her. These are examples of what can be done, but there is still need for a great deal of further progress.
I should just like to say, for the record, that since the establishment of the metropolitan housing authority 13,500 inquiries have been received regarding housing, as a result of which 9,400 applications have been filed. Of these 9,400 applicants, 2,000 have been housed. The authority has about 3,200 applications on file at the present time from persons who qualify because of their need and, their income levels. This shows that an outstanding need still exists for housing units in the Toronto area.
I should like to emphasize that the provision of decent housing is not just a socialist aim. I think it is realized that if our citizens have satisfactory homes which they own themselves they will have a greater stake in our community and in our country, and thereby become better and more satisfied citizens.
I should like to point out, too, that there are many young people who want homes but cannot acquire them because of the size of the down payment which is now required. Many hon. members who have already spoken in this debate have brought this question to the attention of the government. I think it is clear that many young couples who are now renting homes are paying as much in rent as it would cost them to carry the payments on a house if they could raise the down payment. In fact many of them are borrowing money through second mortgages for that purpose. It is true that under the provisions of the National Housing Act they are not supposed to take out second mortgages; nevertheless it is a fact that second mortgages have been registered to cover loans which have been made to enable citizens to obtain these houses in the first place, sometimes at interest rates which are higher than they would be if such loans could be obtained through the government.
I would join with other speakers in asking the government to give consideration to assisting these people to obtain homes. The fact that there are new homes vacant does not

National Housing Act
mean there is no market for them, but suggests instead that there are people who want homes but cannot meet the present requirements. The hon. member for Fort William in his remarks last evening gave an example drawn from his own area.
We must take cognizance of the fact that today many young couples are spending more of their income for accommodation than is normally considered desirable. On the basis of sound financing it is usually considered that one should spend only one quarter of his monthly income to pay for housing accommodation. Many couples are spending more than that. This has resulted in many wives having to go out to work in order to supplement the family income. Sometimes this has an adverse effect on family life, in that the children are not given all the care they require because their parents have to be away from home during the day. This is but one of the side problems arising from this situation.
As shown in the statistics to which reference has been made, in spite of the programs that are in effect we cannot build enough new housing units in all these areas to take care of the need. Consideration must be given to the redevelopment of older areas. I would urge the government to again study means of assisting people in financing older homes. I know this presents a problem because of the condition in which some of these homes may be, but I believe it is a matter that should be looked into once more.
With some trepidation I venture to suggest that consideration be given to another scheme that may help in the financing of homes and over a long period of time assist young couples to buy their own dwellings. I am thinking of a system similar to that which obtains in England. At an early age people put money into housing societies. That money is used for loans for housing, and interest accumulates. I wonder if Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could devise a scheme whereby young Canadians could deposit money with them. C.M.H.C. could lend that money, and an appropriate interest rate could apply to the benefit of the person who deposited the money. Young couples could deposit money to their credit from time to time and over a period of years save up a down payment for a home which they could purchase through the national housing scheme. The same principle employed by credit unions could apply, but on a national scale. I think this would give assistance to those who really want to buy homes.
I close by expressing the hope that the government will continue its good work in

this important field. Although we recognize and appreciate the great assistance the government has given in this realm within the last two years, I hope it will not close its mind to new ideas but will implement other methods that may increase the opportunities for Canadians to purchase homes. I hope the government will continue to give consideration to means of providing adequate accommodation for elderly citizens, and providing rental units for those who do not wish to buy their own homes.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by following the example of those hon. members who have preceded me in offering my sincere and hearty congratulations to the minister on his assumption of the portfolio of Minister of Public Works. Hon. members may not be aware that in Toronto the minister is affectionately known as the cabbage town kid. His background in his riding, his knowledge of the serious social problems posed by housing conditions in certain sections thereof, and of course his familiarity with the Regent Park housing project I believe probably equip him to assume his present duties in a way that few hon. members in this committee are equipped.
I should like to offer some general suggestions and observations concerning this measure, commencing with a discussion of the relationship of housing to the current and increasing problem of seasonal unemployment. It seems to me that the effect of the expenditure of this money can be to contribute to a solution of this problem. An effort should be made to adopt countercyclical measures through housing activity on an annual basis. I have said before in this committee that it seems to me the economy of Canada goes through a recession of sorts every winter. In the allotment and planning of the expenditure of this money we should attempt to have the maximum effect achieved at that time of year when seasonal unemployment reaches its height. Recently in Canada we have adopted proven techniques in winter construction that have permitted building construction to go forward at less cost and greater rapidity than has been possible heretofore.
I should like to offer the suggestion as well that in the allocation of these funds not a rigid but a general priority system might obtain, starting first in the areas with the greatest need in urban redevelopment and slum clearance, and then moving along to low cost and low rental housing, then to limited dividend projects and finally to housing for the lower income groups. In my constituency at the present time there are

I wish to deal for a moment with a most interesting and controversial development which has taken place in my constituency. It involves the use of some land assembly property owned jointly by the federal and provincial governments. A few years ago an extremely interesting social experiment was proposed. It was suggested that the available land be apportioned in the following way. Four hundred houses would be built. One hundred of those houses scattered through the subdivision would be on a subsidized low rental basis available to comparatively large families with low incomes.
This met with unusually strenuous objection from persons in the immediate area who felt they had been misled as to the future use of this land. I have no doubt that some of the real estate salesmen indicated to prospective buyers in adjacent areas that the land would be used for a country club, golf course or something of that nature. I suggested last year that federal-provincial land assembly property should be clearly and definitely labelled so that unscrupulous real estate dealers cannot engage in this kind of activity in the future. In any event it was announced in Toronto that the metropolitan Toronto council has approved this project, and it is now going ahead. I suggest to the committee that this is a most interesting and enlightened experiment. I am confident that within a very few years the success of this project will be demonstrated, and that my constituency will share the credit for having made an important step forward in this field.
There have been rumours and questions in the house concerning the sale of the land assembly units around Toronto, with a view to using the proceeds from the sale of that land for other purposes. I noticed the minister denied this statement when the question was raised, and I would hope he would sustain that position. It seems to me that the concept of land assembly is a sound one, and where possible it should be extended and expanded, particularly in constituencies such as mine.
One other general thought, Mr. Chairman, concerning a matter which has been raised and mentioned by other hon. members, having to do with senior citizens' housing. It seems to me that while the large unit carries with it many advantages, the needs and future of those senior citizens might better be served
National Housing Act
by investigating the possibilities of having more and smaller units, interspersed particularly among suburban areas. It seems to me not a desirable thing that such projects should be so large that the districts around become identified with them. My thought is that in suburbs and in townships such as North York and Scarborough, part of which I represent, it would be a wonderful thing to bring the senior citizens out from the centre of the city and put them in contact with younger families and, in some cases, relatives. Certainly there are occupations they can fill and a need for their counsel and advice. These are some of the functions they can perform. It is fundamental in any approach to geriatrics that a sense of being needed is an essential ingredient in the treatment of older people.
I have one other general suggestion. In dealing with senior citizens and limited dividend projects I would like to offer this for consideration in connection with apartment units. I am wondering whether there cannot be some way by which a series of senior citizens' units could be incorporated into large apartment units, on the ground floor with access to street levels and some sort of garden or common area, where the older people would be with groups in the same buildings, among them young parents with large families who have need for such people to provide such services as baby sitting and care of one kind and another. I know this presents a terribly complicated problem in terms of mortgages, but if some way could be found so that encouragement would be given to the builders of those apartment units, some advantage as far as mortgages are concerned, it might produce a beneficial result.
I just wanted to make a few comments of a general nature at this time, and I conclude by again congratulating the minister and wishing him the very best of luck in his new appointment.

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to add my voice to those who have preceded me in congratulating the minister. I hope his tenure of office will be a profitable one both for himself and for Canada.
There is no need for me, Mr. Chairman, to explain the necessity of housing in a country like Canada, but it is very difficult for me to give some of the opinions that I personally have without emphasizing the necessity of housing to Canadian citizens. It is an accepted fact that the citizen has a right to a standard of living that will be adequate for the health and well-being of his family, which includes food, clothing and housing. In a prosperous country like

National Housing Act
Canada every citizen has a right to a certain economic security, one that is at least sufficient for reasonable stability, the independence of the family and the type of housing that is adapted to the needs and functions of a normal family life.
While the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act facilitated the construction of housing in Canada, and was adequate and entirely satisfactory some years ago, it is only reasonable to believe now that it should have been streamlined to meet the needs of the Canadian public today. Some few years ago it was possible for the individual to buy a house at a reasonable rate of interest, with a reasonable down payment. That condition does not exist today. Conditions have changed considerably since that time.
I am afraid that the present condition is due to the deficit financing which has increased the cost of housing so much that it is not easy for any ordinary purchaser in the lower income bracket to be eligible for a loan, even from the government-established housing institution. To qualify the ordinary individual would need to have a much larger income than is ordinarily given to the average employee at this time. It is my opinion that the National Housing Act, which until the advent of the unadmitted tight money policy was entirely satisfactory to the Canadian public, is now antiquated. It was the duty of this government to streamline it to make it satisfactory and workable for today's conditions.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, as I was saying at one o'clock it is my opinion that it is the duty of the government to streamline the present housing policy to make it workable for today's conditions. While it may not have been the government's intention to capitulate to the lending institutions of Canada who were anxious for a higher interest rate, the conversion loan method accomplished exactly that for the housing industry, which is one of the most important industries in Canada. It is now suffering from the government's action in their conversion loan policy which has automatically created a tight money policy. This has made it impossible to make the proper contribution to the Canadian people and to the housing industry which, as I said before, is one of Canada's most important industries, under our present system of deficit financing until such time as the 
government establishes methods to stabilize a policy of homebuilding to enable the contractor to formulate a program that he will be able to keep up over a 12-month period.
The present instability in the supply of mortgage funds to finance housing at a reasonable rate of interest is creating havoc for the building industry. It is recognized that housebuilding more than any other industry depends on the ready availability of credit. A ready supply of mortgage funds has a marked effect on the rate of housebuilding. This situation does not only affect the housebuilder but it also affects the producer of building materials and also creates a fear in the industry which discourages the development and the introduction of cost reducing methods in both the housebuilding and materials industries. Unfortunately, due to this condition very little research and practically no new building methods have been introduced in the industry in the past two years. This tends to make our present methods partially obsolete and very often defective. The present constantly changing application of our building policy has a disruptive effect and creates a disorderly market.
It is estimated that in 1958 a great number of units remained unsold or unrented. While I did not look up the figures for 1959, I want to quote from an article in the Globe and Mail for Wednesday, January 27, 1960 which refers to 1,000 bungalows which have been left unsold in the Scarborough district. It reads in part as follows:
There are 1,000 houses in Scarborough which should not have been built. They are the wrong size, on the wrong lots, at the wrong time.
The 1,000 houses referred to in the article were built two years ago and $15 million of our tax money was invested in them. The article continues:
They are empty monuments to the folly of a well-meaning, unrealistic policy of central government.
I am told that in fact there are 3,000 to 4,000 additional houses in this project that are not sold. They are not considered as finished houses because in some cases there is a door or a piece of moulding or a sink missing and they are not counted in the 1,000 houses that are unsold. I do not know what the latest figures are in that regard but I am told that is fairly reliable. It is also stated in the article:
Many C.M.H.C. officials are not satisfied with the scheme. They fear that if buyers are found, their incomes will not be sufficient to maintain the homes up to a reasonable standard.
The government should not use the building industry for the purpose of balancing its economy in some sections of the country rather than for the supplying of houses where

houses are needed and where a ready sale can be found for them. This policy will endanger the immediate future of a very important industry whose position at this particular moment is far from being bright. I would repeat that the conversion loan policy of 1957 was an outstanding example of the spur of the moment planning of the present government, even if one were tempted to overlook the $150 million of additional interest that it will cost the Canadian public.
