speechtext: I am delighted to have these suggestions. I am writing them down one by one, but when my friend talks about the conversion loan of 1957 you can appreciate that you are making my task a little difficult. Would the hon. member be good enough to confine himself to the housing issue?

I agree. The only thing is that while the minister was speaking in French he referred to a lamb and I would say that in this case the taxpayer was the lamb, or did I misunderstand? I may not be able to say that the conversion loan had an absolutely detrimental effect on the building industry in Canada but I am at a loss to understand how a prospective home buyer will be able to purchase a house if he is an ordinary worker with an ordinary income. In that regard I should like to quote from the Gazette of Friday, February 12, 1960, where I find the following:
The brief said it takes an annual income of $7,800 for the first five years and $6,000 for the next twenty to buy even a modest home under the National Housing Act. Yet bureau of statistics figures showed the average industrial wage, assuming 52 weeks full employment at only $3,984.
We all realize that the homebuilder, who is after all recognized as an important part of private enterprise in Canada and is entitled to a legitimate profit, cannot, under these conditions, produce a home that the average worker with a low income can buy. Conditions such as those which exist in Scarborough could be reproduced in many places in Canada. It should be possible for a man with a reasonable or modest salary to buy a home under our present housing act.
It is recognized by all welfare associations and all family service organizations that one
National Housing Act
of the most important requisites for the proper upbringing of a Canadian family is proper housing. This condition, which is recognized by all as a necessary requisite, can only be achieved if the government's policies and actions in the housing field are reasonable and make it possible for the employee with a low salary to purchase a home containing the facilities necessary for the proper upbringing of a family.
The present government should not be guilty of using Canada's biggest single industry as a convenient faucet by which to turn on or off Canada's economy, as the trend suggests has been the case. In 1957 the Minister of Public Works announced a multimillion dollar program. However, I am afraid that the conditions attached to the system of direct loans to builders was most unrealistic. Under this program only 25 loans per builder were permitted and these loans applied only to houses of a certain type, with a great number of limitations as to size and the number of bedrooms.
In 1959 a considerable amount of money was made available under a new policy which called for 15 loans to each builder and the restrictions as to the size of house and number of bedrooms still applied. This policy applied to the builder who was able to build 10, 15 or 20 houses and it applied also to builders who were ready and able to build 500 or 600 houses. In order to circumvent these regulations I am informed a great many builders formed a number of different companies so that they could take advantage of as many loans as possible.
Builders generally do not believe that the present restriction on size should apply. They feel it should be changed. It is a recognized fact that the small matchbox type of unit is actually more costly to build than a reasonable sized house. It is for this reason I suggest that housing policy be reviewed so that it can be made to conform with existing conditions, especially with the present cost of land. With the present cost of land, if you put a small house of 1,050 square feet on a 50-foot lot you will eventually end up with a $16,000 house and this is not within the realm of possibility for the average worker in Canada. Looking at it from this standpoint, it is not economic to buy the small type of house and that is probably one of the reasons why a great number of them remain unsold in the urban centres. While this policy may have had the effect, temporarily, of balancing the economy in certain sections, I would suggest that the results are only temporary and are far from being satisfactory.
Direct lending by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was sharply reduced in

National Housing Act
1959, and this affected the policy of the approved lenders who found conditions less attractive and therefore curtailed their activities. May I suggest that the Minister of Public Works immediately make a study of present conditions and face up to the problem in a realistic manner so that some of the following improvements may be made:
1.	The amount of the loan should be increased to enable the down payment to be reduced, and thus have a more realistic relationship to the average income of the average citizen.
2.	The period of the mortgage should be lengthened in order to eliminate second mortgages, along with the fantastic costs of obtaining and carrying them.
3.	Grants should be given to municipalities toward part of the cost of the essential services for housing development.
4.	The policy of charging insurance on the mortgage should be eliminated or changed. I quote a press clipping from the Winnipeg Tribune of January 25, 1960, in which it is stated:
-C.M.H.A. in five years has amassed $60 million from the mortgage insurance system, a scheme designed to protect the lender.
If we have amassed $60 million in five years, then that seems to indicate that this policy is unnecessary. It is also stated in this article that there has been very little in the way of losses. If this fee were eliminated the cost of a house might be reduced by $300 or $400 and this would make a considerable difference. The home owner not only has to pay an unnecessary fee but he has to pay interest on it. Over the life of his mortgage, now 30 years, the cost of the insurance will amount to something like $600. If this fee were eliminated or even partially eliminated we could save between $300 and $600 on the cost of a house.
The minister should give consideration to amending the National Housing Act to enable lower income families to buy houses under terms which would be similar to those pertaining to limited dividend housing companies. The loans available to house builders should be increased, the terms revamped and extended. If all these suggestions were put into effect I feel quite sure that many things would be accomplished. First of all, the housing industry and the house supply industry, which is equally important, would be working on a 12-month period instead of working for part of the year. There would be a lot of interest created amongst the youth in rural areas and they would remain on the farm if these mortgages were extended in rural communities. It is a well known fact that the residents of rural communities are

good credit risks and they should be extended the same advantages as people who live in urban areas.
If the Minister of Public Works will include these suggestions in studies designed to streamline loans to the building industry, then I know the Canadian public can benefit, not only through the effect of these changes on our economy but through the provision for all sections of Canada of the type of housing which I am sure the minister agrees the Canadian people deserve. If the minister will consult a publication issued by his own party at the time of the election I am sure he will find many of the suggestions that I have made are therein contained as Conservative promises. I could quote from the Winnipeg Free Press an article which outlines many of the promises made by the present government in connection with housing. May I suggest that the Minister of Public Works review those promises, make the necessary alterations to our present act, and I am sure every member of the house and every Canadian citizen who will benefit thereby will be very deeply indebted to him.

Mr. Chairman, at this time I welcome the opportunity of entering the discussion on the proposed amendments to the National Housing Act. In doing so, I should like to join with others who have congratulated the Minister of Public Works. I am sure that under his guidance the National Housing Act will serve the public in the best possible manner. I trust also that in certain fields this act will receive his review and reconsideration, and out of this will come an act which will even better serve the communities of this nation and all those who make their homes in N.H.A. structures.
During the past two years an extensive amount of public money has been made available under the National Housing Act, the greatest amount of which has been advanced on the basis now known as agency loans. These are loans which are provided under the terminology of the National Housing Act for essential homes; they are minimum structures. On the average, as we all know, they have a square footage of approximately 1,050. It is in connection with these that my few remarks are going to be made today.
The program to supply this highly essential low cost housing has been extremely worth while. It has served well in the communities of Canada and it has likewise created a great number of jobs. However-and this is something I would ask the minister to consider-it has influenced to a large degree the areas of growth widely known as suburbia. In these developments a number of factors

have become apparent. It is my hope that these problems will be reviewed in the months ahead.
Suburban growth throws great new areas into our metropolitan communities. It throws on them the burden of the extension of services such as water, sewers, roads, sidewalks, hospitals and also, perhaps above all, the cost of education. With suburbia other factors have developed, based upon our essential housing, by providing the only low cost and low down payment accommodation for many of our young couples. They have moved from the centres of large metropolitan areas. They have moved from that situation, which kept them close to their work, out into suburbia with all the wonders it has to offer but also with all its difficulties.
Amongst these difficulties is the arrival of the first child which immediately brings in the need of the family's purchase of a secondhand car or a used car of some type because the little lady has been divorced from her shopping communities. She has been divorced from access to doctors; she has been divorced from access to all the normal functions and services which previously were available to her family living in their older area or older part of the community. All of these problems have been created with the spread of suburbia.
As far as the municipalities are concerned, great problems have also developed. Within the family life, and social practices of the new family units of Canada, part of the responsibility, I feel must be assumed by this House of Commons in the policies which we are now following. How much better would it be for the factory worker to buy an older home in a more developed, more centralized area closer to his work than to move out to a little dreamhouse, a cottage which, although it looks so attractive and is so modern, yet so poorly serves the family needs that he must support and sustain within the limits of his income. I would recommend to the minister that a very thorough study and review be given to this great need. It is growing rapidly in all metropolitan areas of Canada. If possible, amendments should be made in the future to the act to serve this great and urgent housing requirement.
It was only about a year ago that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation requested the lower mainland regional planning board to make reviews of just such matters as I am now discussing and to report to the C.M.H.C. regional office at Vancouver. Most of what I have said was found to be definitely true in connection with their inquiry. Their report to C.M.H.C.-and I read from the Vancouver Province of January 18, 1960- states in part as follows:
National Housing Act
Many potential home buyers find National Housing Act qualifications too strict for their incomes, says the lower mainland regional planning board.
This puts dangerous strains on family life and adds to the civic problems of slums and illegal conversions-
It goes on further to report that in our great metropolitan area in the year 1971 the population of greater Vancouver will be over one million people, a jump of some 40 per cent from the 1961 level. It states:
With this tremendous expansion there is a need for a definite housing study on a metropolitan basis-
That study should be on a continuing level. I will not pursue this matter at too great length because there are many other hon. members who may wish to make a few remarks. However, I hope that our new minister will put this very acute social problem -that is what it is; it is not only a housing problem-on the agenda of matters for review and revision possibly in the future for the National Housing Act.
I should like to pay special attention to certain operations under section 16 of the National Housing Act as it is today in connection with limited dividend housing. Under this and the other programs of land assembly I would commend to the minister a review and if possible an adjustment of the act, particularly with reference to the metropolitan areas. These are both programs which will serve a tremendous need of our Canadian public in metropolitan areas but which today are receiving little attention or indeed in many cases are little known of by civic and municipal authorities. They are programs which aid the housing of our aged people.
Commendable though certain parts of the program of limited housing may be, it is most distressing to us on the Pacific coast, confined as we are between mountains, as our population expansion has created a pressure resulting in higher land costs. Today the picture is that a minimum house under our regulations providing three-bedroom accommodation must rent for $72.50, based on the program set forth under the act. This limits the cost of that property or that home, land and building, to $7,950. The net result is that we do not see growing or being built today housing to supply this requirement.
Some review and some revision is necessary to put this on a more realistic level. I cannot speak of other areas but I can certainly speak of the Vancouver area as my relationship with housing there is very intimate, although perhaps it is more divorced these days when I am serving in the House of Commons. But the last time I had occasion to review the figures I found it would cost

National Housing Act a minimum of $11,000 to provide the accommodation required under the act to make such housing available to people requiring low cost rental propositions. Land assembly is part of an essential program. It could be a means of clearing slum areas and, vacant lands which the local authorities cannot afford to plan for use on a basis which fits in properly with a community program. I again recommend to the minister that he should examine this question because the administration of the National Housing Act is doing too little to carry out this splendid program of land assembly.
I also urge that further effort be devoted to the establishment of low cost rental housing for senior citizens. We have three new units in my own riding, all of them constructed under this plan. They represent a most worthy undertaking and, to give credit where it is due, in addition to advice being provided by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and provision of an adequate mortgage structure, assistance is given in our province to the extent of 20 per cent by a capital cost grant which I can assure hon. members is doing a great deal of good for the aged and those who must live on fixed incomes. I would urge definitely that the minister consider the promotion of this idea -an educational program, if he likes-among service clubs, municipal groups and senior citizen groups in order to bring into being more of this low cost rental accommodation which is so essential.
On mortgage matters generally, I would express the hope that the new interest rate charged under the National Housing Act will result in a more extensive part being played in this field by the conventional mortgage lenders. I know that the minister shares this view. I should be happy to know that a large part of the moneys we are now voting would be diverted particularly to the special types of housing, and I hope our standard mortgage companies will again enter the national housing program in a real way and that a high percentage of the loans made under this act for single family units will be provided by them.
There is a point which must be mentioned while we are discussing conventional mortgage companies, and it has to do with the need to assist young families settling in an older area, in older homes. Today we find that the conventional mortgage companies are completely abandoning this field of lending. A few of the companies do enter the market at a very high rate of interest, but the amount of money they are prepared to lend is restricted to such at pitiful sum that the young family man who decides he must live


near his work and spend within his income finds it almost impossible to acquire one of these older homes. Possibly he could buy one of these homes at $8,900. Through conventional mortgage channels he is able to raise about $3,000, leaving him with a balance of $5,900. His savings are probably no greater than those of a man who has decided to move out to suburbia. He is a sound individual, and let us assume he has only $2,200 in his bank account to pay down. That would leave $3,700 still to be raised, and it can thus be seen that a serious situation confronts this young family. The necessity for a second mortgage arises, and in a growing number of cases unfortunately, even for a third mortgage, on which a discount of up to 35 per cent may be paid. Often, too, there is a five-year call term which completely cancels out the value of any amortization program which the owner may have.
I am not being critical of any one in this house, but I say that by virtue of the fact that we are not reviewing the situation we are forcing the more sensible and the sounder types of our young wage earners into an extremely difficult position. We have to take care that these things which so directly affect our young families are on a basis more sensible than the 10 and 15-year programs which today are the maximum amortized periods a borrower can now get under conventional mortgages.
While I am on this side of the subject, may I say that I have a feeling, which I think is increasingly shared by those whose profession is the real estate business, namely that conventional mortgage lenders generally should consider amortizing their conventional loans on something closer to national housing mortgages, certainly over a period much longer than the 10 and 15 years that is the practice today. It appears to me that it is time consideration was given to altering the statutes governing mortgage and loan companies so that they may be permitted to advance a mortgage on something closer to 80 per cent of the proper appraised value of a property. I think with the security which a mortgage company takes, and based on a proper long range amortization program, there is little reason why the mortgage companies should not be prepared to assume such risks.

I do not intend to make a speech now, but I should very much like to commend the hon. member for Coast-Capilano on one of the best speeches I have heard on this or any other subject for some time. Since we are in committee, there is no reason why the minister should not reply

to some of the points which the hon. member raised without waiting until the debate comes to an end.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, may I just say a few words on this matter, and very strongly urge the National House Builders Association of Canada, in co-operation with the Canadian government, to set up a central mortgage bank. Such a bank would enable small investors to share in the financing of construction, while at the same time receiving higher interest rates.
A fully guaranteed mortgage is one of the safest forms of investment.
It is only through a central organization that mortgages could be converted into bonds of various denominations, which could be purchased by anyone.
However, such bonds should be guaranteed by the government.
The idea is not to change the procedures of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation; it is rather to create a new independent organization which would operate in every province.
Funds for the central bank would be provided by the sale of bonds issued and guaranteed by the government on the basis of actual mortgages. In that way, inactive savings would contribute to the expansion of housing in Canada.
The central mortgage bank would provide very attractive investment opportunities to small investors. Those who get a return of only 3 or 4 per cent from banks or trust companies could get up to 6 per cent.
Mortgage rates might be around 6f per cent.
Collectively, small depositors across the country own a tremendous capital of about $7i billion in banks and trust companies.
The scheme would have a dual purpose: first, to provide needed funds to the home construction industry; second, to provide more profitable investment opportunities to small investors.
The purpose of the central mortgage bank would not be to make high profits, but rather to help taxpayers, because the profits would be strictly limited.
Mr. Chairman, I very strongly urge the city of Joliette to avail itself of the benefits offered by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for slum clearance.
National Housing Act
I know, because I have received a brief to the effect that the syndicats catholiques nationaux de Joliette fully endorsed this suggestion, because slum clearance in any city serves:
1.	To increase the city's assets;
2.	To reduce fire hazards;
3.	To lower interest rates;
4.	To reduce the cost of public relief, and
5.	To provide winter employment to the building trades, so long as demolition work is carried, out on a planned basis.
Allow me, Mr. Chairman, to point to a drawback in the present C.M.H.C. act concerning slum clearance. This drawback does not apply in large cities where apartment houses and accommodation are always available; but in small centres like Joliette, Sherbrooke or others, municipal authorities seem a bit reluctant to undertake slum clearance since the act provides that displaced families must temporarily be housed by the municipality which is covered by the C.M.H.C. act.
I know that this problem does not arise in cities like Montreal or Toronto, but in towns like Joliette and others, there is no surplus accommodation, there are no apartment houses. It is then extremely difficult to house displaced families.
Therefore, I ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) to consider the possibility of including a clause in the act enabling localities with a population of at least 100,000, for instance, to benefit from a special advantage in order to meet the cost of temporarily putting up those displaced families, pending the construction of new accommodation.
Mr. Chairman, I join with all my colleagues in the house in commending the splendid work done by credit unions in the province of Quebec. Much of the housing development that is taking place in cities, and especially in small centres, is due to credit unions.
Before closing, Mr. Chairman, may I mention in this house the benefits derived from the Quebec family housing service which, under the act, promotes housing construction and enables the ordinary Canadian to become a home owner. The government of the province of Quebec, as everyone knows, pays back 3 per cent interest to the buyer. This is a great encouragement to young couples to buy a house. I would have liked very much to hear the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) mention the benefits provided by that act of the province of Quebec. I think it could be cited as an example for all the provinces of this country.

National Housing Act

Would the hon. member permit a question?
Could he tell me why the Quebec government has not granted this 3 per cent refund since the federal law has been enforced?

Mr. Chairman, I may answer the hon. member that this provincial legislation has enabled refunds at certain conditions. It applied only to companies with headquarters in the province of Quebec, and to credit unions. Its purpose was to encourage companies whose head office is located within the province. At that time, there was plenty of money available for loans whereas today there is a shortage of funds and the provincial government amended its legislation so that people who want to come under the act may recover 3 per cent interest.
Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member allow another question?
Mr. Chairman, may I finish my remarks?
No? If you do not wish to answer my question, I have no objection.
I did answer your question.
You did not answer, because-

Mr. Chairman, before closing my remarks, I would like to repeat that the Quebec government has set an example for all other provinces in this country, in offering those advantages to people who want to build a home. Unfortunately, there has been a tendency in certain quarters to discriminate against the province of Quebec, as is being done by some members of the opposition, and to rant against the province, but, in the homebuilding field, and with this interest refund, the province of Quebec sets an example for other provinces to follow.
Moreover, the province of Quebec passed three bills: one to improve housing conditions; another authorizing employers to grant loans to employees; and I wonder whether the federal government might not adopt the same policy with regard to some crown companies. Under that legislation, the lender supplies the funds. The main advantage of this type of loan is that companies operating outside larger centres, because they know their employees' wages, the degree of permanency of their jobs, etc., may grant a higher loan in proportion to the cost of the house, apart from the fact that such loans

would generally be granted in localities where loan companies are not always interested in lending, beacuse of the distance, inspection needs, and so on.
Another provincial legislation conferring special powers to the municipalities has also been passed by the provincial government.
Mr. Chairman, before closing, allow me to say that the province of Quebec has made available upwards of $76 million to help people who wish to build themselves a house. The average age of borrowers is thirty two.
According to the figures showing the number of loans made by companies and caisses populaires in the province of Quebec, the amount of those loans is as follows:

Mr. Chairman, would you allow me to say a word only, because, a moment ago, I asked the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm whether he would kindly reply to a question. He tried to evade the question, because he found it rather difficult to give an answer.
No, I answered it.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm stated that the province of Quebec made a certain refund to citizens who borrowed from companies having their head office in the province of Quebec.
Pardon me, to borrowers who borrow from companies having their head office in the province of Quebec.

That's it. So, would he claim that the Prudential Insurance Company of America has its head office in the province of Quebec? Would he claim that the Prudential Insurance Company of England has its head office in the province of Quebec? Why then, for so many years, has the provincial government prevented our fellow citizens from taking advantage of the federal legislation, a legislation adopted by our government, our Canadian government? That is the question I was asking, and that is the one he did not answer.

Mr. Chairman, allow me, in reply to the question asked by the hon. member, to say this: the former government, when it passed that legislation, did not fully consider the requirements of the average Canadian, while the provincial government legislation is more within reach of large Quebec families.
Nothing is changed in the act. What is changed in the act? Give me an example. Nothing is changed in the act. If you are unable to reply, ask the minister to do so for you.
At present, anyone living in the province of Quebec who borrows money is entitled to a 3 per cent refund under the legislation which has just been adopted.
Why was it not adopted before?
The rate of interest has gone up since-
