speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Chairman, the National Housing Act, perhaps one of the best pieces of social legislation passed by the former Liberal government, was designed to help people in the moderate and low income brackets to have their own home.
Any member who represents as I do a working constituency can fully appreciate the importance of that act. When you give a worker an opportunity to own his own house, you make him more conscious of his duties as a citizen, thus enhancing his contribution to the community. That was the primary objective of the act. This objective was not easy to fully achieve from the start, but up to 1957, there was evidence of direct progress towards the proposed target.
Unfortunately, the government, particularly in the past, appears to have completely lost sight of the primary objective of the act.
We are getting farther away from it from year to year. While the National Housing Act has social implications, it must be realized that it is totally dependent on the country's economy. No other act, I think, is more exposed to contingencies resulting from poor
National Housing Act
administration. And with credit restrictions, high interest rates, generally rising costs of labour and materials and sky-high speculation on land, it is no longer possible to say that we are satisfied with present conditions.
This is another field, apparently, where the government has missed the boat, because today, whether we like it or not, we have to admit that high mortgage rates and present costs of residential construction are far beyond the financial capacity of most Canadian families.
That, in my view, is the result of the muddled policies of the government, which has been forced, by circumstances of its own making, to raise from 6 to 6f per cent the rate on mortgages granted under the National Housing Act. Nor can the government lay the blame on the Bank of Canada or on chartered banks, because the decision was made by the government itself; and the necessity for that decision arose out of the government's tight money policy.
The result is that small investors will find it increasingly difficult, if not impossible, to face the obligations involved in purchasing a house at this time, and the very people who should benefit from the act will be deprived of such benefits in the future.
I have read many reports from builders associations containing comments on their activities for 1959 and their estimates for 1960. The minister will forgive me, but as far as objectivity is concerned, I much prefer their views than the speech he made when he introduced his resolution. If I read that report correctly, the year 1959 was not as good as the year 1958 in the field of construction and, according to estimates based on actual figures, the year 1960 will not be as good as was 1959.
I shall quote now from an article in the Citizen of January 28, 1960, where, under the title "Fewer new Homes in 1960", we find a report concerning the city of Ottawa:
(Text):
A 25 per cent reduction in proposed new home construction in Ottawa during 1960 was forecast last night by D. Roy Wymark, retiring president of the Ottawa real estate board.
(Translation):
The forecast is that, in certain regions, the proportion of the decrease in housing construction will reach 30, 35 and even 40 per cent.

National Housing Act
I have here an editorial from La Presse for December 29, 1959, which clearly states the present difficulties. This is what it says: Contractors rightly wish to maintain their industry in full activity. But this industry has been so active in the last 15 years that large sums of money have been tied up in buildings erected at a record rate. Funds available for mortgage loans are becoming scarce. They have also become scarce for another reason; because billions of dollars have gone into government borrowings, either to make up for its heavy deficits or for its famous conversion operation of two years ago.
Mr. Chairman, with the help of all this information gathered here and there, from builders or from those who study these questions, we can conclude that the year 1960 is starting under the sign of anxiety, because the government has not given to the application of this National Housing Act what it needs most, that is stability. It is all very well to put considerable funds at the disposal of future buyers, but what will happen when those sources are exhausted? It is the government's duty to find an answer, in providing this act with the stability it needs.
Residential construction should be able to rely on a regular flow of funds to acquire the stability which is vital to its operation.
I agree with the suggestion made in certain quarters-the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) also mentioned it earlier-that is the establishment of a mortgage bank. Such a bank would make mortgages negotiable for small investors who, otherwise, keep their money dormant in bank accounts, without any benefit to the community.
Such a bank would be established to release capital already invested so it could be reinvested in construction.
I hope the minister and the government will see the advisability of considering this project. The establishment of this mortgage bank might provide the stability resulting from funds that are regularly available to the buyer.
Of course, the National Housing Act plays an extremely important role in our economy. It can help stabilize related industries, as well as the labour market. It is too bad that the government deliberately restricted credit and by its detrimental money and fiscal policy, opposed the very purpose of the National Housing Act.
Those are the general remarks I wanted to make at this stage of the resolution; I

may have other questions to raise at other stages of this bill.
Before concluding I would like to ask two questions of the minister, and to have his comments on them.
I have noticed that, according to a report issued by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, of all the loans made both by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and other lenders, 20 per cent were made in the metropolitan area of Toronto, while only 7 per cent have been made in the metropolitan area of Montreal.
I would like to know how the minister can explain that in 1958-I do not have the figures for 1959-the metropolitan area of Toronto, with 1,400,000 people, has obtained 20.2 per cent of the housing loans, while the metropolitan area of Montreal, with its half a million people more, obtained 7.2 per cent of those loans.
These proportions, given in a breakdown made by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, show that aggregate loans made in Toronto amount to $179,534,000 and that loans made in Montreal amount to $63,714,000.
I would like to have some comments from the minister on this matter and I ask him to explain this disproportion between loans made in Toronto and in Montreal.
(Text):
I understand that the minister may not be an expert on housing but after all he is surrounded by experts in his department and I would be much interested in having his comments on the disproportion of loans between the metropolitan regions of Toronto and Montreal.
The second point I want to raise and on which I should also like to have a few comments from the minister has to do with the choice of the notary in the province of Quebec when a citizen wants to borrow from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. According to reliable information I have received, I understand that when a prospective borrower applies to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation a notary is designated by the Minister of Justice. For the present, I have no criticism whatsoever to make with respect to the choice of the notary but I want to inquire about this point. When a borrower is effecting 15 loans, do 15 notaries have to be appointed to study the titles and make the individual loans with

the result that costs and fees are increased? If so, I think there is some ground here for criticism. If the minister does not have the information at hand I should like him to inquire and answer later. If the situation is as I have outlined it surely something should be done to avoid the unnecessary multiplication of costs and fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, every speech made in this debate has been of great benefit to me and I am sure to the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It has been a great experience to see that at least in this part of my duties the debates have been non-political. First of all I want to pay my tribute to the hon. member for Nipissing and the hon. member for Levis who over the years have manifested a great interest in housing. I have derived much benefit from their observations.
Rather than repeat what I said in opening when I made a 40 minute speech outlining the reasons why the government is taking this action I am going to confine myself this afternoon, in order that we may proceed as far as possible and complete the resolution and the bill, I hope, to answering the questions that have been asked and to do so very briefly. The hon. member for Nipissing suggested that parliament was being asked for $500 million so that there would be funds available to take us through the next election. All I can say to the hon. member is that in 1954 the former government had an amount of $250 million voted and by the time the election rolled around in 1957 it had only spent $100 million. I think the hon. member for Levis, who understands something about housing, knows how embarrassing it is to have a certain sum of money voted and then to run out in a certain month of the year before parliament convenes again to make further funds available.
The hon. member also asked whether the government would announce its direct loan policy now, and I think that we can pretty well do that. It is a question, of course, for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to work out the allotment of our funds. We are going to be very much restricted this year in comparison with previous years but the main purpose of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is to help the man in the low income bracket as much as possible. To this end, when a person goes for a loan to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation he will
National Housing Act
first be asked to look at the 82,000 homes that are still in the process of being built, at the end of the year, and he will be asked to look at these and see if there is not a house about ready to come on the market that will suit him as a prospective home owner.
Second, the prospective homebuilder will be asked to go to one of the approved lenders under the National Housing Act and, if possible, get a loan at per cent. Then, failing that, the prospective homebuilder comes to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for a direct loan, and whatever we can do for him will be done.
If we are going to be inundated with a tremendous number of applications-there is no indication at the present time we are and if the money has to be allocated-this is all subject to further research during the course of which I would be glad to have the assistance of my hon. friends from all parts of the house-we would then want to ensure that the person who could least afford the extra money should get the loan from Central Mortgage. This would mean people with an income of $5,000 or less would have a preference at Central Mortgage. The other people, with higher incomes, can better afford to get a loan from the approved lenders and those with larger incomes still may get loans very readily, of course, at increased interest rates from the conventional lenders.
We hope, in some way, to allocate the money across Canada, and this will be done as fairly as possible having in mind the fact that ever since we came into office this government's policy has been to protect and to help those in the lower income bracket.
I wonder if the minister, before he moves on to another subject, could say how much of this $500 million it is expected will be lent this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It is a difficult thing to prognosticate at the present time. Last year we lent between $330 million and $340 million. This time we would hope to lend about half of that amount, in other words between $150 million and with limited dividend projects added, up to $175 million.
Is that owner-builder, that sort of application and the direct field as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The hon. member asks about builders; as I indicated in my opening remarks we are, as in former years, making direct loans only to prospective home owners. There will be, at this time, no builders' loans, nor have there ever been at the beginning of any year. We do not pretend to be in the

National Housing Act
business of making loans to builders. During the last three winters we have made loans to builders in order to give winter employment a boost. We do not know whether or not that will be done again this fall or whether it will be necessary. It certainly has had a great effect on employment in this country over the past few years. At the present time we have no intention of making any loans to the builders, and that is the policy we have followed in each of the past three years. When the fall comes, if the situation warrants it, that matter may be reconsidered.
The amount of those loans, then, would be in addition to the $150 million or $175 million to which you have referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Our hope was that this year the total money expended by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would be between $150 million and $175 million.
Does that include direct loans that may or may not be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It includes everything. Another suggestion in which many hon. members joined was that the federal government should participate in slum clearance by increasing its contribution from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. Do hon. members not think the federal government has gone a long way in raising it to 50 per cent? It is 50 per cent at the present time. Some of the provinces participate in these projects by giving 25 per cent, and that is certainly the case in Ontario. If the federal government were to increase its contribution for what has been described as slum clearance-I do not like that word-[DOT] to 75 per cent then that would take away the initiative, responsibility and good judgment of the municipality. We must depend on the municipality to use its best judgment and direction in connection with slum clearance. If the federal government put up 75 per cent of the money and they had to put up only 25 per cent one could not expect a great deal of consideration to be given about where slum clearance took place. The difficulty would be that private interests, running up against the municipality, might be given a preference. In any event, we have a 75 per cent contribution from the dominion and the province in the province of Ontario.
Is the minister not aware of the fact that the municipalities, mayors and reeves, have asked for this degree of assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Yes, we are aware that a great many municipalities have asked for a great many things. We are very sympathetic to all the requests. The trouble we have, as most hon. members will appreciate, is in finding enough money to go around to grant all

these requests. At the present time, rather than increase our percentages we should like to find some way of at least holding the line.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked the question, what are you doing for the lower third of the income group. Let me just stress briefly the history of the National Housing Act in this connection. N.H.A. loans to people with annual incomes of less than $5,000 have increased from 11,900 in 1957 to 17,558 in 1958 and to 24,200 in 1959. Since we have come into office we have more than doubled the amount of loans to people in the low income bracket, that is below $5,000.
So far as limited dividend projects are concerned, since we took power we have completed over 10,000 limited dividend projects. As all bon. members of the house know, and this will answer a great many of the questions, limited dividend projects will serve almost any of these special groups to whom reference has been made, that is the elderly, the young and the man on the small income. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano made some very searching remarks in this connection. Any group of wealthy citizens or public group of citizens who wants to get 10 per cent of the necessary money together could start a limited dividend project and the government would lend 90 per cent of the cost of that project. The rents are very low indeed. They are limited and checked by inspectors from Central Mortgage. In my opinion this is a very excellent way of helping people in the lower income bracket.
As a matter of fact, under ordinary circumstances-and this holds true across Canada-one cannot get into a limited dividend project if your income is in excess of $3,600. If your income goes up to $4,500 during the period you are there, you will be asked to get a house elsewhere. You are considered able to afford something better than a low dividend project. But we are building these projects as fast as we can. We have many others under way and we encourage people to make applications for loans. Of course, in this coming year or in the present year we shall have a limited amount for this purpose. We trust that the good work along this line may be continued.

Would the minister explain that statement? He says he has a limited amount. What does he mean? Does he mean that he is going to deny loans below what he could probably do last year in this field of limited dividend corporation application?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I think this year we expect to make loans of somewhere about $25 million which would be about the same as we spent in the year 1959.
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano also suggested-I think it was an excellent suggestion and many other hon. members made the same suggestion, including the hon. member for Davenport, the hon. member for Scarborough, and several others; if I have omitted any names I must be excused- that it would be an excellent thing if the government could make Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans to renovate old homes. That would be a good idea. But, as I say, the government's lending facilities are limited. Is it not better that we should create new housing units rather than improve old ones? It is new housing units that we require and more a multiplicity of housing units. I should point out to hon. members that if one wants to improve an old house and the newly wedded couple needs this, it is possible to get loans from the banks. In this connection may I say that many millions of dollars have been lent-I think the total is about $162 million-for what are called home improvement loans. They are loans up to $4,000 to improve old houses.
I appreciate, as do other hon. members that it would be very nice to have enough money available in order to build all the new homes we want and to improve all the old ones. But at the present time with the shortage of money to build as many new homes as we should like to build, do you not think it would be better not to divert any of that money to improving old homes, particularly when the home improvement loans are available?
I have also been asked-I think it was by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam- whether or not the government intended to wait to see what the approved lenders will do before making direct loans available. I can say that if this bill is passed today, government loans will be made available tomorrow. I had hoped, since this resolution was introduced on February 4 last, that we would have been making loans at least three weeks ago.

I wonder whether the minister would just permit me to make the observation that last night again-for the fourth time-when we were inquiring from this side of the house what the business was going to be for the next day, members on this side have suggested that the housing legislation be given priority. I can think of the occasion last evening. I can think of the occasion on March 7. I can think of the occasion on March 1 and I go back again
National Housing Act
to February 26. I therefore hope there is no attempt to leave any impressions that members on this side of the house have prevented this housing legislation from being brought down shortly after parliament began its session on January 14 last.
Mr. Pallet!: Your actions are different from your words.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I am making no suggestion that anyone is responsible for it. I am simply answering a question. However, the first suggestion I heard that this housing bill which is so dear to my heart should be proceeded with was made by the Leader of the Opposition three days ago or perhaps it was four days ago.
Perhaps I can help the minister by putting into the record other dates.

I asked three
weeks ago.
Mr. Pallet!: And then proceeded to talk for two or three weeks.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: An hon. member asked many interesting questions and one of them was about the increase in the interest rate. I do not know whether or not he is now satisfied that the interest had to be increased. I was shocked as I read the figures last year to find out how the volume of loans from approved lenders just went down and down so that by the time I became Minister of Public Works the approved lenders on whom we count for so much of our money for national housing loans practically stopped lending at all. It was a very sad situation. It was a difficult thing to arrange a rate of 6f per cent. We wanted to make the little man see he would have to pay as little as possible by way of interest charges and yet we had to raise the rate to a figure which would attract back into this market of N.H.A. loans the approved lenders, and it was a very difficult thing to arrive at a rate. All I can say is that we took the best advice we could get. We have a magnificent organization in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We canvassed the situation outside and we arrived at the rate of 6J per cent. We have confidence that this rate will attract the approved lenders back into the field.
Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Certainly.
I did not want to interrupt him. He is doing very well. However, he changed the rate. What was the date of the change of the rate? Was it November or December?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
It was December 17.

National Housing Act
As a result of the change in the rate, what increase in loans under the approved lenders' scheme has been demonstrated in relation to last year, so that we can see the result.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, if he has seen the figures, the response up to date has been minimal. There is no question about that fact. It has been minimal for several reasons. In the first place, after they have been out of the market for about six months it is a very difficult thing to convince these approved lenders that the time is now ripe to come back in again. We also know this fact. At the present time mortgage companies, insurance companies and the loan companies are for this current year 1960 making their allocations. In other years we had higher returns at the present time because the allocations were made in- the fall. It takes two or three months to get the thing rolling.
Although the figures were very disappointing in the month of January-one would almost feel that the rate of 6f per cent was not as attractive as it should be-the figures, hon. members will be glad to learn when they are published, and I will bring them to the attention of the house, were very much better. In the last week or so they are even better still. As a matter of fact, we are somewhat relieved and pleased to see that the approved lenders are again back into the market. There are other reasons, of course, why they might be inclined to hold back. There are 82,000 houses in the course of completion. They must be disposed of. We have had a very hard winter and the prospective home owners are not busy certainly around our place. It is hard to get out of the house much less than go and look at some new prospect. There are many reasons why the market in approved loans has been somewhat slow in getting started. Does that answer the hon. member's question?
Would the minister mind putting the figures on the record now? I refer to the loans that have been made by approved lenders in January and in February, as compared with last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Yes. I will send up for them. I am sure I have them here. I will put those on the record before the debate is through. I shall be delighted to do so.

The minister asked
whether or not that answered my question. I think another pertinent question related to our present discussion is that among the approved lenders we can assume, can we not,

that the chartered banks are no longer in the scheme of things. Is that so in relation to, say, a year ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Compared with a year ago, the hon. member is quite right. The banks are among the approved lenders. As the hon. gentleman knows, the banks have many calls on them for money and the National Housing Act is only one of them. The banks are guided as to their loans and the percentage they can charge by the Bank Act, and that act confines them to charging a rate of 6 per cent. This has been government policy, and it has been so declared. It is a matter which transcends the duties of the humble Minister of Public Works. The Bank Act is reconsidered every ten years. I think the hon. gentleman was a member of the government, or at least a parliamentary secretary, when it was last revised.
The Bank Act fixes the rate at 6 per cent and, it is very interesting to note the government has received no request from the banks to increase the permitted rate to 6;j per cent so that they could lend money under the National Housing Act. Even if such a request were made, it would be beyond my duties as Minister of Public Works to deal with it. That would be a matter of government policy. I would think a careful second look would be necessary before one would interfere, since to raise the bank rate above 6 per cent in the isolated case of N.H.A. loans would be to encourage other branches of the banks' activities to seek increases in their permitted rates. I think the hon. gentleman is right in his understanding that the banks will not be participating except at 6 per cent, and there are loans going through at 6 per cent to regular customers.
As to the figures, last year the loan and trust companies made 579 loans during the month of December. This year they made 117 loans. In January of last year they made 516 loans. This year they made 140. In February of last year they made 1,043 loans and this year, 550. During the week ending March 4-and these are the latest figures I have-319 loans were made. Last year there were 116. So they are finally taking an interest in this sort of thing.
That is the group outside the chartered banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Quite so. On the other hand, last year the banks made very substantial loans up to this time, but this year they have been negligible.
Would the minister give the figures for the bank loans in January and February of this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In December, 17 loans; in January, 11 loans, and in February six loans.
That is compared with what, a year ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Compared with 900 in December, 670 in January and 883 in February.

Would the minister mind telling me how he reconciles the figures he has just given, which show that the banks are doing practically nothing, with the statement he made some minutes ago that the banks are performing their function of making loans to their regular customers?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I did not say any such thing. If I did, I should be taken to task. What I said was that in spite of the fact that the banks are only getting 6 per cent they are making some loans to regular customers. As can be seen, the number of those loans is very small indeed and the regular customers, as I understand the position, are turning to other approved lenders to get loans formerly made by the banks.
I want to tell the hon. member for Levis that I agree with his contention that the caisse populaire at Desjardins has done a good job. I wish we had more co-operative institutions like that. They are very practical in their outlook and show an interest in the mortgage market which contributes to the social welfare of the people. They take particular interest in the small wage earner, and in that way their efforts are co-operative and along the same lines as those of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
In this connection I suggest that it is the government's hope that in the coming years a secondary mortgage market will be developed. There is a great opportunity now for a secondary mortgage market. For a long while there was not enough difference between bond interest rates and mortgage rates to make worth while the establishment of a secondary mortgage market. Now there is sufficient difference with the 6J per cent that the companies can get on N.H.A. loans, to warrant a company selling bonds to the public with insured loans security. I trust a lot of encouragement will be given to any such ventures.
Does the government intend to extend any such encouragement?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Central Mortgage and Housing is answering all inquiries and giving all the assistance it can by way of advice. We do not intend to guarantee any such companies. We have our hands full making our own direct loans and insuring the approved lenders' loans.
National Housing Act
The hon. member for Fort William complained, quite properly, about the large down payments that are sometimes necessary. He will be glad to know that the average down payment on direct loans through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is $2,500. The average down payment in the case of approved lenders is higher, however, and, of course, on conventional mortgages the down payment is substantially higher still.
The hon. member for Fort William and many other members suggested that we should drop the insurance program. The hon. member suggested that this amounted to $300 on a loan. It is hardly that. It is 2 per cent, which would amount to roughly $260 on a maximum loan of $12,800. I would point out to the hon. member for Fort William, who has always taken a sympathetic interest in housing, that if we did this we would be cutting off our funds established to deal with defaults. We now have an insurance fund amounting to $61 million. That is not a very large fund in relation to more than $3 billion worth of loans insured by the government. We might consider that the United States government, which has been carrying on a housing plan-though not one as good as ours-for a much longer time has been charging double this premium until recently, when the rate was cut. After 20 years they are still adding to their insurance fund, and in my respectful submission it would be bad economics all around to cut out the 2 per cent insurance premium which has to be paid here.
I wonder if the minister would let us have the number of defaults in the past five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: So far defaults have been very small indeed. We do not expect to have any defaults as long as this government is in power because we shall always have a situation where the country will be fairly prosperous, and we are now entering upon what may be the most prosperous year in our history.
With 800,000 unemployed?
How many defaults have there been in the last five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I will send for the figure. There have been surprisingly few.
The hon. member for Kootenay West who lives in baronial style on his great estate out in Kootenay, and who perhaps could be referred to as the squire of the House of Commons, does take a genuine interest in the Canadian people and I admire him for that. He has suggested that greater attention

National Housing Act
should be paid to the small man, the little man, the humble man, the man of low income. I would respectfully suggest to the hon. member that if he will go over our figures and read my opening remarks and the remarks I have made today he will find that that is exactly what we are endeavouring to do, take care of the man of low income.
The hon. member for Quebec West made an interesting contribution to the debate and also suggested that we take steps to assist the man of low income. In the hon. member's constituency of Quebec West which I have visited we have a magnificent example of a limited dividend project and, provided we can work it out, we would like additions made to it.
The hon. member for Kootenay West and others, including hon. members on this side of the chamber, suggested we should make our houses more attractive and offer a wider variety of designs. We do not have at the moment any designs for the log cabin style of house in which the hon. member for Kootenay West seems to be interested but we have obtained at considerable expense and great trouble 97 small home designs. Most of them are published and set out in booklet form. The housewife and prospective home owner can examine this booklet and order any design. All the plans for the house selected will be sold for the modest sum of $10. Great interest has been shown in these designs and thousands of the plans have been distributed throughout the country.
The corporation conducts competitions, belongs to many organizations and conducts research with a view to learning how we can improve the small home and so far we have been very successful.
Several hon. members on the government side have asked if Canadians could build their own homes. Of course they could. Anybody can build his own home if he meets the minimum standards established by the national building code of the national research council.

Mr. Chairman, not long ago I asked for a copy of the plans for the so-called lowest cost approved home from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In its reply the department gave me information about the lowest cost home but there was no indication what the approximate cost of construction would be in any specific location. Could the minister give me that information?

I regret to inform the committee that the minister's time has expired unless the committee gives

unanimous consent for him to continue. Is it the pleasure of the committee to give unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I have one question to ask but I do not want to interrupt the minister if he wishes to continue to develop the theme he is dealing with now. My question is unrelated to it and could be deferred. I do not want to interfere with what the minister has planned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I will just complete what I was saying, if I may. I have in my hand a pamphlet describing the minimum house costing $5,000. The pamphlet gives all the details. This unit was carefully planned and at one time was called the fisherman's house. It is a complete house without a cellar, of course, and without certain plumbing facilities. We have plans for homes in every price range and suitable for every locality. The problem is that in the large urban centres the cost of a lot is so high that it becomes impractical to build a cheap house on such an expensive lot.

I can see immediately, Mr. Chairman, that the minister in referring to the pamphlet he has in his hand is referring to something that was not sent to me in the mail. I received a large booklet. Perhaps the minister would be good enough to identify the pamphlet relating to the $5,000 home so I could obtain one later.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
This is C.M.H.C. No. 1247. It is called the National Housing Act minimum house. I will see to it that my hon. friend gets all the material he can handle, and then some.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont asked about housing starts in Toronto and Montreal. Montreal has done a marvelous job in housing during the last few years and in the year 1959 forged ahead of Toronto. In 1958 there were 26,198 housing starts in Montreal and 24,301 in Toronto. In 1959 housing starts in Montreal were 20,939 but in Toronto they had fallen to 18,774.

Perhaps the minister would permit an observation. I did not have in mind loans under the C.M.H.C. but the overall funds available for construction in Toronto which has always been so much ahead of Montreal. Could the minister give us an explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The reason Montreal and Quebec have lagged behind Toronto has been

because the caisse populaire has made substantial loans outside the N.H.A. The provincial interest rebate has not been available tor N.H.A. loans in Quebec and Montreal.
I wish to commend hon. members from Toronto ridings for the keen interest they are showing in this matter. I would like to do all the things they suggest. I would like to help young couples and old couples obtain better housing more easily, provide better homes and bigger loans and all that sort of thing, but we have to help first those who need the help most. We have to make our money go as far as we can and at the present time we cannot enter the field of making loans available for the mortgaging of older homes.
Before taking my seat I want to thank hon. members for granting me this extra time. Let me say that the winter housing program has been tremendous this year. As I said 82,000 homes were in process of being built at the turn of the year. We know what the unemployment figures are but they would have been so much worse without this construction activity which provided employment to 250,000 men. By that I mean
150.000	men were employed on the sites and in taking material to the sites and
100.000	were employed in factories and warehouses producing materials for these homes.
By the end of October of last year 19,000 loan applications had been received by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the winter program which required us to stop taking applications. This winter's program has afforded work for 52,000 men, of whom 35,000 were employed on site. Thirty five thousand were producing materials, making a total of 80,000 who obtained winter employment.
As the minister, let me say this. In Central Mortgage we have done an extraordinary thing in housing. We have risen from $100 million in loans, the amount lent when we took office in 1957, to $1 billion at the present time. We have as well provided over 10,000 limited dividend units, very low rentals; we have as well 5,000 subsidized housing units where people who cannot afford to pay the rental are helped by the federal government paying a subsidy of 75 per cent and the provincial government 25 per cent.
We are very happy to say that since we came into power 400,000 houses have been built in Canada. It is not an exaggeration to say that there are tens of thousands of people, young families, middle-aged families and old families living in their own houses, modern in every way, who would not have been able to afford houses had it not been for the advent of the new policy of the Diefenbaker government.
National Housing Act

Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister an aspect of this matter of housing administration that seemingly has not been discussed as yet. The minister may recall that on January 19 he made a reply to certain questions I asked him. These questions were:
Has the federal government received representations from any municipal body or city council, requesting the federal government to include a no discrimination provision in all National Housing Act transactions and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans, to prevent discrimination against such persons because of race, colour or creed?
If so, from whom were such representations received, and what reply was made to the representations?
The minister replied and acknowledged that there had been representations, and observed that they came from the Windsor city council. In reply to the request involved in the question the minister incorporated in his reply the letter which he addressed to Mr. J. B. Adamac, office of the clerk, city hall, Windsor, Ontario. I do not propose to read all of the reply of the minister, except to comment on one or two paragraphs. In the fifth complete paragraph, toward the middle, the minister wrote:
As the corporation is not a party to transactions between builders and purchasers it does not exercise control over the terms and conditions of sale which might be prescribed by a builder.
Certainly I would not quarrel with this statement, but it seems to me it does not really touch the heart of the problem. The minister goes on to observe:
Any attempts to take such action by the corporation, might be construed as violating normal property and civil rights; the corporation will be placed in the position of attempting to dictate the conditions by which a builder may sell his housing units.
On the recital of the facts as set out in the words of the minister which I have just quoted and his interpretation of the effect of the property and civil rights clause of section 92 of the British North America Act may be correct. But that is not, I think, addressing oneself to the complaint. The minister points out in the third paragraph:
The corporation-
When I use the word "corporation", of course, I am referring to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I continue:
The corporation includes in its construction contracts a clause providing that the contractor shall not refuse employment to anyone on the grounds of race, national origin, colour or religion.
That is, of course, the fact, and it is satisfying to know the origin and the date of the legislation providing for that particular provision; but it seems to me this very provision serves as a precedent for the minister to really

National Housing Act
try and deal with this question of discrimination, which in a number of instances which have been brought to my attention, and which I know have been brought to the attention of the minister, present a situation which is not theoretical but actual. Then, in the fourth paragraph of the letter to Mr. Adamac the minister says:
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in insuring loans made by lending institutions under part I of the National Housing Act, or making direct loans available, does not discriminate. It is primarily concerned with the ability of purchasers to meet their mortgage payments.
It is true, as the minister says, that the corporation does not, in the making of direct loans, discriminate; that is clear, but that, too, if I might suggest to the minister, is not evidence that the minister really addressed himself to all aspects of the complaint involved in the representations which have been made by the city of Windsor.
On March 1, as I understand it, the national committee on human rights of the Canadian Labour Congress made representations to the minister on the broad aspects of discrimination. They point out in this brief, a copy of which I have had sent to me, that the federal government did in 1953 enact a fair employment practice act and that six provinces have enacted fair employment practices acts; that in addition four provinces have enacted fair accommodation practices acts, which provide a prohibition against racial discrimination in public accommodations. The fact that they have provided prohibition against discrimination in public accommodations is not an argument in favour of the position that the federal government has no means of acting in respect of a matter which I am sure concerns the minister, just as it does any other hon. member in this house. It is because I believe that is his view that I am seeking today to persuade him to give further consideration to the reply be made to the clerk of the city of Windsor and which, I presume, he made to the committee on human rights of the Canadian Labour Congress.
This committee points out further in its brief to the minister that the bill of rights, which was introduced last session by the Prime Minister-and presumably the bill of rights to be introduced this session will be in the same terms-provides for the right of the citizen to the protection of the law without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex. I refer to part I, clause (2) (b) of the bill introduced by the Prime Minister in the last session of parliament.
It seems to me, if we are determined to provide in a bill of rights against any violation of human rights, that in so far as this

parliament can in respect of matters over which it has in any way some element of control, attachment or jurisdiction, we should seek in related legislation to take steps consistent with the general concepts and purposes which are proposed to be embodied in the bill of rights. But altogether apart from whether we are to have a bill of rights it seems to me that we must take steps to avoid discrimination against anyone by withdrawal of the benefit of an act of this parliament even though the other consequential benefits may result from contractual arrangements made by one individual with another, altogether apart from the legislative embrace.
I would not have mentioned the case by name but since this has now been done in these representations made to the minister on March 1, I would direct his attention to the fact that in the submission reference is made to the Watkins case, as it is called in Windsor, arising out of a situation which took place there in July, 1959. There a respected citizen of Windsor, Mr. Lloyd Watkins, a young Negro draftsman, was refused the opportunity to purchase an N.H.A. guaranteed home because of his colour. This case was referred directly to the minister's department not only by the complainant himself but also by the city council of my city. The representations in part are as follows:
We assume the facts of the case are known to you. It should also be mentioned that the city council of Windsor has requested appropriate action under the National Housing Act to ban discrimination in publicly guaranteed housing.
Then, on pages 3, 4 and 5 a number of other cases of discrimination all over the country are listed, cases arising out of circumstances in principle not different from those in the Watkins case. The committee on human rights of the Canadian Labour Congress made a proposal to the minister and this is found on page 7 of their representations. They say:
We propose that an. amendment be inserted in the National Housing Act prohibiting racial discrimination in respect of any property which is processed under the act. The amendment could contain a provision similar to that found in the fair employment practices and fair accommodation practices acts. It should stipulate that no one enjoying rights and privileges conferred by the National Housing Act may discriminate in the sale and rental of buildings and self-contained residential units in multiple dwellings erected thereunder, on the grounds of race, colour, creed and place of origin.
Then they point out that violation on the part of anyone should result in a denial of future benefits to the offender. It is suggested that the minister should be empowered to communicate the names of offenders to the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
lending institutions involved with instructions that they be declared ineligible for further loans and benefits under the act.
It is argued there, and I will be very interested in listening to what the minister or the law officers of the crown have to say, that the authority of the federal government to act in the area of housing does not arise from any legislative power inherent or directly given in the British North America Act but rather arises out of its ownership of money and its corresponding right to spend this money as any other institution with its resources may. The right to refuse to deal with racial discriminators, it is suggested, is just as constitutionally valid as the right to refuse to deal with delinquent builders.
These are the arguments presented. I wonder whether the minister is prepared now to deal with this situation in a way that will satisfy hon. members of the house that every step has been taken to avoid discrimination along the lines suggested and if that is not the case perhaps we could hear from the minister as to what steps he proposes to take. In any event, it seems to me that at a time when we are discussing and talking about human rights it will be difficult to convince the Canadian people that this parliament has not the authority in respect of a matter over which it has an interest and which, if exercised, could avoid the discriminations about which complaint has been made.
I bring this before the minister at this time because of the deep feeling over this situation in my city, one where we have a spirit of tolerance between racial groups, between white and coloured people, on a scale which I think is emulated in no other community in Canada. I hope the minister will be able to give me a reply that will satisfy my own concerns in the matter and those of thousands of other people in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to be able to control acts of discrimination across Canada. My field is pretty well confined to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and national housing and I can say with pride that to my knowledge there has been no example of racial discrimination at any time since we took office on any of our projects or any venture undertaken by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We are very proud of that. As a matter of fact, we are also proud that the president of one of our federal-provincial projects is a negro, and I can assure you that he is a very good president. May I also say that we have 79951-0-126
National Housing Act
taken the most strenuous and rigid means to stamp out any possibility of racial discrimination.
On our insured loans anybody can get a loan. When we consider approved purchasers anyone, regardless of race, colour or religion, can get a loan. On our limited dividend projects there can be no exclusion of anyone for any of these reasons. With respect to federal-provincial projects, in my own riding, for example, I think we have most of the races represented in the federal-provincial project in Regent park. We have a wonderful group and a great spirit there. In our slum clearance developments we are bound to see that people whose places are acquired are re-established, and they are reestablished regardless of their colour. There is no discrimination in our department.
I should like to go further and extend our power. We make approved loans and we make direct loans. A contractor who is building for us cannot discriminate when he builds because we have a clause in the contract and if he discriminates for reasons of race, colour or religion, we cut off his contract. But when an approved lender makes a mortgage loan and we insure it or when we make a direct loan the question is how far we can go in checking up and policing the builder or owner as to discrimination when selling on the ground of race, colour, language or religion. It is a very difficult thing to do, and as my friend points out, under section 92 of the British North America Act we have no control dominion-wise over property and civil rights.
In the last six months I have been endeavouring to find a clause to put in the mortgage that we could make stand up and that would provide that as long as money was owing on the mortgage we could see to it that there was no discrimination. As a matter of fact, I have asked the Department of Justice to give the matter further consideration to see if we can avoid what my friend describes as having happened. Fortunately, it has not happened, except I think on one occasion, in so far as any national housing loan is concerned. If we could even stop that one occasion, we would be glad to do so.
I want to assure my friend that the labour congress made a very telling representation. I was very delighted to see them, and to assure them that the matter was under constant consideration. If I could find some clause to put in the mortgage that would hold water -my hon. friend from Essex East, who is a good lawyer, knows what I mean by that -I would do so. It would be a fatuous thing

National Housing Act
to put in a clause merely for the sake of putting it in, without it being valid. If I could find a valid clause to put in to control these builders, buyers and sellers, then I would be glad to include it.
Could the minister give me an answer to my question as to how many defaults there have been on N.H.A. mortgages in the past five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Since 1954 there have been 55 claims totalling approximately $552,591, and for 1959, the past year, $375,424, on 36 claims. If my friend so wished, I could give him the details of those claims.

Several hon. members have congratulated the minister upon his appointment to his office. I will not go that far yet. I hope that perhaps a year from now I will be able to do likewise. I was interested in listening very closely to the minister's reports, especially in the last few minutes. I share with him the congratulations to the previous minister upon the very vigorous action he took and I also share with the minister the sorrow which I believe he expressed over the situation since he has taken office. This is no reflection upon the minister at all, but I would say it is a reflection upon the Minister of Finance and the policies which, unfortunately, he has forced upon too many departments in this government.
There are many aspects of this particular housing problem, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to confine my remarks today to one particular aspect and that is the need for slum clearance which is so evident in our urban areas. I am very pleased to notice that both the government and the opposition-I mean the official opposition-are recognizing that slum clearance is a problem for which the government should take some responsibility. I recall that back in the 20's the popular thing to do was to ignore the fact we had such a thing as slums. We believed we should shut our eyes to them and refuse to believe they were there. They felt that unfortunately the slums, like the poor, will always be with us. Finally, we realized that we could not just close our eyes and believe everything was rosy because, no matter how tight we shut our eyes, the slums were not only there but tended to spread. We began to realize that unless some vigorous action was taken they would spread like a blight right across our cities.
There have been sporadic attempts in the past by various private enterprise organizations to try to meet this problem, but they have been nothing more than drops in the sea of blight. I think one of the biggest dangers

resulting from these attempts has been the creation of this picture that this problem was being met when quite the contrary was true. Even the stepped-up activity we saw in this Department of Public Works during the last couple of years under the direction of the present Secretary of State for External Affairs has not resulted in any rapid rate of slum clearance. The slums are still gaining on us.
I think that possibly one of the first wrong impressions we should clear from our minds is one to which possibly the minister made a reference when he said that the government should not or could not under present circumstances, with the tight money situation as it is, take up mortgages for improvements on old buildings. He felt they must concentrate on new buildings. Old structures, as such, are not the cause of this blight; they are only the effects. There are many old homes which are just as comfortable as any of the new homes that are built today. I think anyone who studies this problem thoroughly can find the underlying cause for these slums which blight our cities, and I refer to improper use of land and improper planning for the future of the city. This is the underlying cause of our slums.
Whenever we think about tackling this problem we always think about the terrific cost. The minister has said today, we would like to do this, we would like to build more homes, we would like to clear up these slums, but think of the terrible cost. I wonder if we have ever associated the cost of these things with the many other costs of our civilization which we are accepting day by day. I should like to just tally up some of the subsidies we are now paying in connection with these slums, federally, provincially and municipally. Have we ever stopped to tally up the amount of money that is paid into these welfare or service organizations; into our fire departments and police departments, whose major use is in connection with these slums; have we stopped to tally up the cost of fire insurance rates which are raised to abnormal heights because of these fire-traps, and which add to the cost of everyone who insures his property? Have we ever stopped to think of the costs involved in thefts and burglaries which are committed by people who have been raised in these slums? Do we think of the cost of maintaining our penitentiaries which have to be built to house and maintain the products of these slums? We have been neglecting, for far too long I would say, the fact that the cost of trying to correct this problem, staggering as it may seem, is nothing compared to the cost we are now paying to maintain these slum areas.

If I may I should like to deal for a moment with these costs which frighten us when we consider tackling this problem. How can we lower these costs? I have here a book entitled "Urban Renewal", by Reuel Hem-dahl. I would highly recommend this book to anyone who is interested in this problem. Here, on page 33, he says:
In order to provide housing for people who need it, at least five alternatives are available:
1.	Reduce land and building standards, so as to lower housing costs to the price level of the low-income groups.
2.	By voluntary methods, reduce the profits, if any, of subdividers and builders.
3.	Introduce efficiencies into the home construction industry.
4.	Increase the purchasing power of the low-income groups.
5.	Provide housing with government subsidy.
Just for a moment let us examine the five alternatives he offered here. I can say in all honesty that he is not suggesting these alternatives, he is merely pointing out that these are the only alternatives by which we are going to get cheaper housing. The first one is to reduce standards. 1 do not think that is a desirable thing. The minister mentioned today one area at least where something could be done along this line. He mentioned that, even with the present low cost house the greatest difficulty they meet is that of finding a lot in any of our cities on which to build. In most of our cities the cost of the lot alone would be in excess of that of the house that is going to go on it. Surely, having regard to the standards of our homes and our houses in this country, before we embark on a policy of reducing those standards we want to make sure that at least if they are going to be reduced from the present level they are not reduced beyond the point which allows for the creation of a proper home or we might be in fact adding to the blight which exists already in far too many cases.
The second alternative to which he refers is that of reducing profits voluntarily. I do not think that is a very realistic one. I do not think you would drum up much support across this country in any endeavour to embark upon a voluntary plan that is going to reduce profits or wages in the building industry.
The third possible plan has some merit. It refers to the introduction of efficiencies into the home construction industry. One way in which it can be done is by larger scale organization, the standardization of parts and attendant factors. That is something that has always been ignored in the past. Less than 7 per cent of our houses today are built from prefabricated materials. I think possibly this is one field that could 79951-0-126J
National Housing Act
be explored to a much greater extent. As far as our housing field is concerned, we have always insisted on having custom-made homes. Something that is custom-made in any other field of manufacture is considered to be a luxury item. There are not too many ordinary people who go out and buy a custom-made car. They do not buy custom-made clothes unless they are like me and are of a size which compels them to do so because they cannot get a suit of their size in the regular field. Housing is the only place where we still insist on having something custom-made. One building can have as many as 50 different special trades and special contracts. All that is accomplished is to build up a whole group of little vested interests, each one of which is more interested in maintaining its position than it is in the over-all welfare of the Canadian people having regard to their housing.
The fourth alternative is to increase purchasing power. That is something that is possibly outside the ambit of the subject before the committee at the present time. It also is a desirable end and is something the government should keep in mind as an objective at all times.
The fifth one is to provide a subsidy. This is something that has been done by governments, both this one and the ones we have had previously. But I wonder whether they have applied it in the proper way. In looking at the record today, I wonder whether they have not, in far too many cases, failed to help the situation but rather have confounded it or in other words done just the exact opposite of what they set out to do. It is not going to help too much to have one little job done here and one little job done there if cesspools of slums are allowed to grow up all around them and finally to envelop them.
I see that my time is just about up, Mr. Chairman and I shall be obliged to curtail my remarks today. If this government just want to play at this thing, they can keep on in the way we have been going in the past and they will obtain just about the same results, and we shall never meet the situation and make any attempt to conquer it. But if they want to cure this situation, the government is going to have to take a much longer range view than we have ever taken in the past. They are going to have to go into this problem in all its aspects much more closely than we have ever done previously.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed that all the 73 divorce bills listed under order No. 71 be taken at once?

I do not think so, Mr. Chairman. With regard to Bill No. SD-19, which is the one listed first, my participation in this particular bill in this particular matter is occasioned by the invitation I received from
Private Bills-Divorce
the Minister of Public Works at a previous sitting to engage myself in discussing these particular questions and applying ourselves to understanding what is contained within them and just what the committee, at this stage, and parliament, later on, is being asked to do.
Unfortunately, I am not a member of the committee of the house which considers this particular type of bills and accordingly I have not had an opportunity of seeing what went on and how extensively the committee considered all the questions before us now and that were dealt with in the private bills committee. However, as I read the evidence in this particular instance it would indicate that this is one of those types of cases that I have heard referred to as open and shut. That is, no private investigators are involved. No private detectives are involved in any of the investigation processes prior to determining whether or not there is a case for the granting of divorce. It indicates that there is an admission by the respondent in this case and by the corespondent that they were living together as man and wife and consequently in the course of that living together they had committed an act of adultery which lays the ground for a divorce being granted.
There are apparent a few inconsistencies in the different parts of the evidence submitted, and so far as the evidence that I have from the Senate subcommittee on divorce is concerned it does not clear up those inconsistencies. I would like to refer to them and ask the sponsor of the bill whether the committee which undertook to consider this matter thought they were of importance in this particular case or whether no attention was given to them.
In the prayer with the petition-not in the prayer itself-it is indicated on page 5 that the respondent-I will read the sentence-a Mr. Kerr, now residing in Montreal is employed as a foreman. The relevant part is his employment as a foreman.
Further on in the evidence the question is put to the respondent who indicates that his occupation is that of salesman. I suppose it is possible to be both at the same time. During the interval between the middle of June 1959 when the petition was signed and the end of January 1960 when the respondent appeared before the committee I suppose there may have been a change of occupation.
There are three daughters in the present case, aged 21, 11 and 9. It may be that the eldest is married or about to be married. The father made fairly substantial contributions toward their support. At page 10 of

Private Bills-Divorce
the evidence the petitioner is questioned by her counsel, Mr. Cohen, as follows:
Q. Does your husband support these children?
A. Yes, he gives me $100 a month.
Q. Has he made any other contribution to the family?
A. Yes.
Q. Could you tell this committee what it is?
A. Approximately $5,000.
Q. Has he paid any of the medical bills for the children?
A. Yes, at one point $500.
This is substantiated by the respondent who when being questioned by Mr. Cohen used the same figures. I assume the payments were made for the period of time the husband and wife were not living together. I could find no reference to any financial arrangements to apply after the divorce is granted as I assume it will be. It would be difficult for a woman to raise two or three children on the general salary she could command. Would the sponsor of the bill tell us what, if any, financial arrangements were made for the continued support of the children?

I am discussing only Bill No. SD-19 at this stage. I propose to ask questions with respect to other bills. We could deal with them one at a time if that is the normal procedure.

speechtext: I object to their being taken en bloc. I thought it was understood that they would be taken individually as has been the practice.
