speechtext: Very well. We will discuss Bill No. SD-19. Shall clause 1 carry?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Skeena raised two questions. He asked first about the fact that the wife described her husband's occupation as salesman and he referred to it as foreman. This is not an extraordinary event and perhaps the easiest way to explain it would be to say that a husband may describe himself as a sanitary engineer and his wife refer to him as a garbage collector.
The other question concerning arrangements for financial support after the granting of the divorce is one that is outside the jurisdiction of the committee. Members of the committee of the other place were sat upon when they attempted to raise questions about financial arrangements for the wife and children. These are matters for provincial jurisdictions and court procedures are available to people in this position in the provinces.
May I point out that the minister reversed the description of the occupations in referring to them.
Mr. Chairman, the hon member has threshed that straw a little more fully than I had.

I was merely attempting to assist the minister, taking the advice of the Minister of Public Works who is not in the chamber. I was helping him get the facts correct.
It seems odd that divorce for Quebec and Newfoundland is within the jurisdiction of this parliament but that an important condition relating to the granting of the divorce, financial arrangements for the support of wives and children, should be considered outside the jurisdiction of parliament. If such is the case, then we should certainly take the next step and remove divorce from this house. If we are not going to do that, then we should not deal with one-

I have to raise a point of order. We are clearly not discussing a particular provision of Bill No. SD-19; we are entering into a very general debate on divorce. There are bills on the order paper which will be coming up for second reading and also one resolution, I believe, and certain private bills. I am sure the house can arrange to have a long debate on divorce, but in committee we are confined to the facts with relation to a particular bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I agree that the hon. member was not discussing the bill before the committee; he was replying to some observations. I thought he would come back to the bill; I was going to rise and call him to order but I am sure he wants to be relevant now.

Mr. Chairman, I apologize if what I said was not relevant to the bill. I was dealing with this particular bill and with the evidence as I read it before on pages 10 and 11, answers to questions asked of the plaintiff and of the respondent. These questions and answers relate to financial support of the children. In this particular case, where reference is made in the evidence to support of the children up to this particular time, it would seem to me that we should concern ourselves with the support of those children following this time. Here are two children-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I think the objection raised by the hon. member for Halifax to discussion of the financial responsibility of the children or of the wife is well taken. This comes within provincial jurisdiction. Even if we wanted to enter into this question

it would be outside the power of this house; therefore, I do not see the utility of discussing these matters.

With all due respect, sir- and I certainly do not want to run foul of your rulings or of your ideas or of the objections of the hon. member for Halifax-in this bill we are asked to dissolve this marriage and say that henceforth it shall be null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever. As we have done in other cases, I think we are entitled to wonder about the results of our actions. We are being petitioned and asked to nullify a marriage and to grant a divorce. As you say, sir, after the divorce takes place the financial matters are within the jurisdiction of the province itself. But we should have some conscience and we should wonder about what we are being asked to do and what possibly will be the result thereof. It was in that light that I was dealing with the question of the financial arrangements and financial support for the children, following the passage of this particular bill and the granting of the divorce itself.
If those financial arrangements were in effect prior to the request for divorce, or prior to the petition being granted, if we have no right to discuss, to speculate and to suggest that this should be considered, I can only hope that the father will be somewhat more generous in the future toward the children than he has been in the past. I think we all agree that the people who are affected to the greatest degree by this action which is asked of us are the children in the family. These are the ones who may be subjected to the most serious consequences in so far as our action is concerned.
I have no more particular comments to make, Mr. Chairman, although I repeat that in this particular case, if because of divided jurisdiction, we are forbidden to speculate upon what financial arrangements may be made for the children, following the granting of the divorce, then we should take steps either not to grant the divorce or to take the whole question out of the hands of this house and put it in the hands of the provinces where they have ample jurisdiction already.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to say something in support of what the hon. member for Skeena has said. It would seem to me that in this particular case we are again being asked to grant a divorce. It is a divorce that would lend itself to speculation that an arrangement had been made and that collusion may have been entered into. We can come to that conclusion without too much stretching of the imagination, and I think that
Private Bills-Divorce
is borne out by the evidence we have. This evidence was taken in the main by nonprofessional men in a committee that is not constituted as a law court or has not the ability or the resources of particular law courts.
The bill is numbered SD-19, and is No. 28 of the Senate. I am wondering what has happened to the reports in between SD-19 and No. 28 of the Senate.
In this particular case the man obviously has allowed the woman to do the petitioning, and the husband has done the honourable thing in making it possible for her to obtain this divorce on the only grounds that the Senate committee will allow as grounds for a dissolution of marriage.
It has been pointed out that in this particular case a settlement has been made. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the settlement of $5,000 is not sufficient to take care of the children. There were three girls of this marriage. One of them is of marriageable age and probably is married by now. The settlement of $5,000 would indicate to me, Mr. Chairman, that there had been some discussion about the termination of this particular marriage, and this is borne out by the facts in the evidence. If this is true, Mr. Chairman, if there is any doubt in any hon. member's mind that this divorce is not as it appears in the evidence taken by the committee of the Senate, then obviously we should not endorse any action that would indicate that legalities have not been complied with, and arrangements have been made to obtain this divorce. If we do not believe that, then we should object to these arrangements being made. I think we have an obligation to see that these arrangements are not made and we should pass legislation that will prohibit the making of unnecessary arrangements that were not made known in this particular bill.

Again I must raise a point of order, not to quarrel with some of the statements that have been made, although they are obviously at variance with the evidence, but simply that the hon. member for Timiskaming is dragging this debate down that well-known C.C.F. garden path, and I do object. Last week the chairman told us that we were to confine ourselves to discussion of the marital offence which could lead to divorce. He said that was the sole matter of debate, and I must protest and raise a point of order this afternoon.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I can recall very vividly the former prime minister of Canada, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, explaining to us the whole basis on which these petitions come before us. He put it very briefly and yet very effectively

Private Bills-Divorce
when he said that the individual citizen was exercising his prerogative to appeal to the toot of the throne for legislation to supply a measure of relief. If that statement of the former prime minister is in essence what is taking place, then I humbly submit that this committee has every responsibility to consider all the implications of what it is being asked to do. It behooves the committee not only to consider whether or not adultery has been committed but also to consider all implications of the action it is about to take. That includes the future welfare of the family who will in effect no longer have either a father or a mother, as the case may be.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Further to the point of order, it is my opinion that we cannot separate these bills from any other bills brought before the house. If this bill concerned a telephone company there would be wide latitude given in the discussion of the bill itself. Hon. members would want to know where the telephone line started and where it went to and how the company was financed. These facts would all be pertinent to the bill. I suggest that these bills are just as important to the people concerned as a telephone company bill, an oil company bill or any other bill that is brought before the house. I think the house is going to have to make a decision before long. If the house is not going to treat these bills as regular bills then a decision will have to be made as to their presentation in a different manner.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the point of order is a very important one. I place some value on the comments made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, but if any other hon. member would care to comment on this point before I make a ruling I would certainly appreciate it. It may be that it would not be relevant and proper to discuss the legal consequences of the divorce because this is a matter which comes under provincial authority but at the moment I cannot see that it is not relevant to examine all the factual circumstances of each case. I would be obliged to rule to that effect unless I have more assistance from those who oppose this view.

May I speak again to the point of order? There is a committee set up to deal with divorce cases known as the miscellaneous private bills committee. Two members of the C.C.F. party belong to that committee. One of them has taken part in the debate this afternoon and the other one has made a sudden foray on the scene. I suggest to Your Honour that there is full opportunity to discuss the matter of the occupation of the husband or wife, which has been dealt 
with here this afternoon, the ages of the children, which has been dealt with this afternoon, and whether the paying of $5,000 in medical bills on behalf of the children constitutes collusion, which one member of the C.C.F. says it does and another member says no. All these things have been dealt with this afternoon.
When anybody comes to the foot of the throne as it were and asks for relief they should be accorded the utmost respect and their problem solved if possible but I do not think anybody should come to the foot of the throne and then have a large foot planted in their backside from the corner of the house from which all these questions have been raised this afternoon. There is a time and place for everything. As long as I have been here the practice of this chamber has been to stay away from other matters apart from the direct question of adultery and the proof that is adduced in support of it. It is our duty to examine that proof and decide one way or the other and unfortunately we do discuss these matters here before the public. People's names are mentioned which is perhaps one of the unfortunate things in our process.
But we do have a system whereby we can look into these divorce cases. The public can attend meetings of the standing committee if they desire. The C.C.F. members can attend those meetings too if they want to and bring up the questions that they are now trying to bring before us.

On the point of order, these bills are in no sense petitions to the foot of the throne. The fact of the matter is that under section 91 of the British North America Act legislation regarding marriage and divorce is given to the government of Canada. It is true that before confederation some provinces had divorce jurisdiction and their jurisdiction was recognized. For instance, in the case of the province of Ontario the parliament of Canada granted the right to deal with divorces. But our rights stop with marriage and divorce. The parliament of Canada can annul or dissolve a marriage but the parliament of Canada has no jurisdiction whatever to deal with the children of marriages, even much less than to deal with what may happen to the wife. The parliament of Canada has nothing to do with that.
My submission on the point of order is that all these remarks with regard to deals made with respect to children or deals made for maintenance of the wife are completely irrelevant and have no place in this debate whatsoever.

I should like to comment on the point of order and some of the references made by the hon. member for Halifax. I am not sure whether he was referring to the remarks I made or the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming or whether he was referring to the remarks of each of us and got them mixed up. He made some comment about a $5,000 payment for medical bills being some sort of payment resulting in collusion. In the first place, the medical bills were $500, not $5,000 and I made no such reference to $5,000 in medical bills. If he was referring to the hon. member for Timiskaming, he did not make any reference to $5,000 in medical bills either. He made reference to a $5,000 payment which was referred to in the evidence.
But the hon. member did raise a question which I think is extremely important for us to consider. As I understood his suggestion, he said that these matters are referred to the miscellaneous private bills committee, that that is where they are dealt with and considered and that is the only place they should be considered. In fact what he is suggesting is completely contrary to the rules of the house as they apply to legislation, whether public bills or private bills, of which this is one.
The rules, which apply to all committees, provide that if we refer bills or special matters to committees it is for the purpose of the committee being able to consider the matter in an informal manner, to have witnesses appear and so on. But invariably it is not the exclusive right of any committee of the house to make decisions. Committees are only an extension of parliament in a smaller form with a smaller number of members participating and in all cases committees must report to parliament upon their activities and at the same time make any recommendations they may wish to make. That is the case with divorce bills.
Certainly the miscellaneous private bills committee has considered and dealt with these questions and now, following the rules of this house which have been in effect for many years, is reporting back on a particular bill and is, in fact, recommending that certain action be taken. This committee of the whole has every right, I think, to go into the evidence which has been considered on some of these questions by the miscellaneous private bills committee, and also has the right to go into questions which the miscellaneous private bills committee might not have gone into.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must say that some of the statements made by the member for Skeena were out of order, but I am not convinced 79951-0-127
Private Bills-Divorce
that a discussion of the particular facts connected with each bill is not permissible. Before I reach a final decision on this I would have to examine the matter further to be sure that I would not deprive any hon. member of his right to discuss the bill as completely as he wished. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Thank you for your ruling and your consideration, Mr. Chairman. As I say, in this particular case we have the proposition put to the committee that there had been an amount of $100 paid toward the support of the wife and additional medical expenses had been paid by the husband from time to time. It does not say that this was done as the result of a court order, but by agreement. On page 10 of the evidence we find these questions and answers:
Q. Does your husband support these children?
A. Yes, he gives me $100 a month.
Q. Has he made any other contribution to the family?
A. Yes.
Q. Could you tell this committee what it is?
A. Approximately $5,000.
Then to make sure that this was not confused with the money paid for medical bills, a further question was asked:
Q. Has he paid any of the medical bills for the children?
A. Yes, at one point $500.
I am suggesting to this committee that there is an indication there has been an agreement by these parties to the obtaining of this divorce. If that is true-I do not disagree that it should be done, I do not disagree that these people should be divorced- I am just thinking of the legal requirements with which one must comply in obtaining a divorce-
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes.

Does he say that if a couple have been separated over a period of years and the husband is paying toward the wife's support when divorce proceedings are taken, that is collusion? Does he know what collusion is?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am not a lawyer. I would appreciate it if the hon. member told me what collusion was in legal terms. I do not know, but it is my understanding that collusion exists where arrangements have been made between two parties to do something that is not necessarily in keeping with the law in order to obtain something that is

Private Bills-Divorce
legal and which, if it were done by arrangement, would prohibit them from obtaining it. This is my interpretation.
In many of these cases-I cannot find it in this one and probably that is an oversight on the part of counsel-a question is asked, have you lived with your husband, and if you have not, have you had any relationship. This question is asked, then, has there been any agreement in the obtaining of this divorce. If the answer were yes, and the lawyer always tells them to make sure there has been no agreement, I would suggest that this would be collusion. If the case were tried in a court, the court would have to throw it out. Now the other committee did not necessarily have to do this, but in so far as my understanding goes, it would constitute collusion. It does not come within the legal definition of it, I suppose, but in my opinion it is an indication of it. I would suggest that these people have had a fairly close relationship and when the trouble, in the form of medical expenses arose, the husband was quite willing to make a contribution of $500 toward meeting those expenses. Now he is making a contribution of $5,000, which would prompt us to think there has been a settlement in this case.
The members of this committee who belong to the legal profession may disagree or they may not, but I would suggest that this is an indication of collusion. In other words, the question usually asked is, has there been any arrangement in the obtaining of this divorce. In this case, the question was not asked, but if it were and if an honest answer were given, I suggest it would have had to be yes, that there was some form of collusion. This situation has been developing over some period of time.
One of the faults with this particular procedure is our inability, in discussing the matter at various stages, to refer it to such organizations as are available to outside courts-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

Probably because of my complete ignorance as to what the legal terms are, this discussion arose as a result of a question that was asked. The question was, is there any hope of reconciliation, and the answer was, absolutely none. This question was of concern to the Senate committee and I would suggest, therefore, it is of concern to us in discussing this bill. I am only suggesting that courts have other methods of dealing with this particular question. A question is asked, is there any hope of reconciliation, and I would suggest that in every case that comes before a court in the province of Ontario in which this question is asked the court will refer the people to the welfare agencies that have been established in the province for that purpose.
I do not think it is sufficient for us only to ask the question. I think we should also give some guidance and some assistance through welfare agencies in our procedures to see whether we cannot make a success of this marriage rather than grant a divorce.

speechtext: Order. The hon. member is not following the rule. As I indicated, if the hon. member's remarks are not strictly relevant to the matter before the committee I shall be compelled to ask him to resume his seat.

I should not like to remain on the record, which could be read by people who do read Hansard, some remarks indicating that there was any collusive factor in this case. The fact is that the respondent's husband has been living with another woman as man and wife. That is not a strict legal term; it should be concubine and paramour or something like that, but we call it man and wife. He has been doing that for over two years. He has in the past looked after his family even though he has not lived in the common domicile or the common home and there is every indication that he will do so in the future.
My hon. friend pleads ignorance of the law and I know he would be the first to recognize that he is probably guilty of that

ignorance. When you use words such as "settlement" or "collusion" or terms like that, you use terms that can mean only one thing. In this way the whole type of debate tends to put blots on people who are almost helpless to protect themselves against this thing which we have been going through here during the last three private members' hours.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before the hon. member sits down may I ask him a question? Granting the fact that the one party to this action was living with another woman for two years, if the husband had made an arrangement with his wife and paid a cash settlement of $5,000, what is the situation in legal terms? I am asking the question in a legal sense. Would collusion not have taken place no matter whether there was adultery?

The answer is obvious. If there was an arrangement between the parties that he would pay her money only on condition that she sue him for divorce, that would obviously be entering into adultery on the consideration of divorce. But that is not the case here. For some time the husband had been looking after his family while living with and supporting another woman. That sort of thing is not collusion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member answered only part of the question. I should like to ask him this question. Is it not collusion in a case where there is an arrangement?
This is outside this case entirely. There is no suggestion here of any arrangement whatsoever.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am suggesting there is an arrangement for $5,000. In not answering the question directly I think the hon. member is agreeing that if this is my contention I would be right in saying there was collusion.

I cannot allow that statement to pass without comment. When I get up on my feet here to state my mind on the affairs of these unfortunate people I give my honest opinion and I am never going to deviate from that course in this House of Commons. I think that is an unfair allegation to make, namely to suggest that I agree with the hon. member to say something entirely different.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in this particular case the hon. member has pointed out that the question was not collusion but is whether the divorce should be granted on other grounds entirely? If this is the situation, I do not disagree with him. But I think we should not temper our desires for the end result. After reading this case 79951-0-127i

If that is the case, I would suggest that this divorce bill should be passed by the House of Commons with an amendment that there was not adultery in this case but that we give relief to the people because they are no longer living together.

speechtext: I think it may be said that we have made some progress today in connection with the business of the house. With that thought in mind, perhaps I could ask the house leader what he intends doing on Monday and as much of next week as he can indicate.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The proposed agenda for next week will run in this way. Monday will be private members' day. Then I have seven items of business here which we shall try to take up in the order in which I give them, subject of course to change with due notice. On Tuesday we will start off with the report of the Canada Council to be referred to the public accounts committee, followed immediately by the public accounts and the Auditor General's report to be referred to the public accounts committee. Those are routine proceedings and last year they occupied the time of the house for only about, I would say, five minutes. Then we will go on with second reading of the bill to amend the National Housing Act which we were on today followed by the setting up of the committee on defence expenditures. The next item after that would be the federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements bill in the name of the Minister of Finance. If we get through those items, then we have the resolution in the name of the Minister of Public Works concerning the trans-Canada highway and the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport concerning the amendment to the Railway Act. Some of these items may be altered during the course of the week, but those are the matters we should like to deal with, and in the order which 1 have outlined.

Might I ask whether the government has given any further consideration to the action it intends to ask the house to take on the capital punishment bill? This question is now in a state of suspended animation, but there are reports going around that the government has dropped the idea of proceeding with it. The opposition has been very co-operative, and I think I am asking a fair question. In the meantime, in the absence of action from this house, two persons have been hanged, and I would like the leader of the house to indicate how he would like the house to proceed with the debate on capital punishment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would appear to me that the question is not proper at this time, because the leader of the house has just given the program for the coming week. This is a question which it would be more appropriate to ask on the orders of the day. However, if the leader of the house wishes to reply-

On the point of order which you have raised, it is a practice of long standing that the leader of either of the opposition parties has the right to put questions when business is announced by the leader of the house. That is very much in order. I have put the question to the hon. gentleman and I think he owes it to the house to give some reply with regard to this matter of public interest which is very much in the minds of the people of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The matter is under consideration, but I know the house is anxious to press on with some of the legislation that is on the order paper. This will not prevent subsequent consideration of the debate on capital punishment at a later date.
Does the minister mean there will be a request for further consideration at a later date? I would hope so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

When?

Never.

1.	No. There are 11 weekly denominations and four semi-monthly equivalent denominations leaving seven weekly denominations for which there are no semi-monthly equivalents.
2.	When a claim for unemployment insurance benefit is made, semi-monthly stamps have to be translated into weeks-first to determine if a claimant is eligible for benefit, next to determine his weekly rate of benefit and lastly to arrive at the number of weeks' duration to which he is entitled.
In making these calculations the unemployment insurance commission found that in numerous instances the employer had affixed the semi-monthly stamps in the employee's insurance book improperly. This required frequent references back to the employer to ascertain the correct pattern of the insured person's employment; and in other cases, where the error was not detected at the time of calculation, subsequent adjustments had to be made as the result of complaints lodged by claimants who had been paid at lower rates or for lesser periods than those to which they were entitled.
Moreover, the four denominations that were withdrawn represented less than 5 per cent of the total annual sales of stamps, whereas the weekly equivalent denominations amounted to 40 per cent of the total annual stamp sales.
The withdrawal of semi-monthly stamps in the lower denominations has enabled the commission to dispose of claims promptly in a situation where time is of the essence.
